parole.significato: Abstract noun suffix; forms part of larger suffixes and exists on its own especially as a suffix added to compound word…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian -ъє (-ʺje), -ьє (-ʹje), from Old East Slavic -ьѥ (-ĭje), from Proto-Slavic *-ьje. Doublet of -ие (-ye), a borrowing from Church Slavonic.

parole.significato: used to form feminine deverbal nouns denoting a result, process or an abstract concept
forms feminine nouns of both animacies
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-aga. Compare Russian -ага (-aga).

parole.significato: Suffix appended to words to create a masculine noun, usually denoting a result of an action or an object.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ajь. cognate with Serbo-Croatian -ај m, Russian -ей m anim (-ej).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-aľь. With -ь m (-ʹ), cognate with Polish -al.

parole.significato: Suffix used to form verbal nouns from verbs; added especially to verbs ending in -ати (-aty) (alternatively -яти (-jaty…
parole.testo: Rebracketing of -ння (-nnja), from Proto-Slavic *-nьje. Compare Russian -ание (-anije), Belarusian -анне (-annje), Polish -anie.

parole.significato: appended to verbs and nouns to form masculine agent nouns denoting profession/occupation; -er, -or
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -арь (-arʹ), from Old East Slavic -арь (-arĭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ařь, borrowed from Gothic -𐌰𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃 (-areis), from Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz, borrowed from Latin -ārius, a nominalization of -ārius, from Proto-Italic *-āzios, from Proto-Indo-European *-yós.

parole.significato: Appended to nouns to form feminine inanimate nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ara.

parole.significato: adjective-forming suffix, added to nouns (especially body parts), indicating having the property of that noun, particul…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-atъ / *-astъ.

parole.significato: Suffix added to some perfective verbs of to produce imperfective equivalents.
Suffix used to form adjectives from nouns, meaning "having X".
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic -атъ (-atŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-atъ. By surface analysis, -а (-a) + -тий (-tyj).
Inherited from Old East Slavic -ачь (-ačĭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ačь.

parole.significato: Suffix appended to words to create a masculine noun, usually denoting an animal or a person who does something, perform…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ašь. Cognate with Bulgarian, Macedonian, Russian, and Serbo-Croatian -аш, Czech -áš, Polish and Hungarian -as (noun-forming suffix). Compare Romanian -aș, Greek -άς (-ás).

parole.significato: Combining form used to form imperfective counterparts of prefixed derivatives of бра́ти (bráty, “to take”).
parole.testo: From imperfective lengthening of the Proto-Slavic perfective infinitive stem *-bьr- (from the infinitive *bьrati) + -а́ти (-áty). Compare Russian -бира́ть (-birátʹ), Belarusian -біра́ць (-birácʹ).

parole.significato: Uncommon suffix used to form collective nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -ва (-va), from Old East Slavic -ъва (-ŭva), from Proto-Slavic *-ъva.

parole.significato: -ing, -ence, etc. (suffix used to form abstract nouns from verbs)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-tvo.

parole.significato: Uncommon suffix used to form nouns from verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-vo (neuter of *-vъ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-vъ, from Proto-Indo-European *-wṓs. Cognate with Lithuanian -us (Etymology 4) via Proto-Slavic *-vъšь, past active participle ending. Compare Russian -вши (-vši), see also Polish -wszy.

parole.significato: Used in combination with prefixes to form imperfective verbs with an approximate meaning “to clothe, to dress, to put o…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dęgati, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ-, *dʰn̥gʰ- (“to cover, conceal”). By surface analysis, дягти (djahty) + -а́ти (-áty). Cognate with Lithuanian deñgti (“to cover, to dress”).

parole.significato: Used in combination with prefixes to form perfective verbs with an approximate meaning “to clothe, to dress, to put on”.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dęgnǫti, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ-, *dʰn̥gʰ- (“to cover, conceal”). Cognate with Lithuanian deñgti (“to cover, to dress”).

parole.significato: Used in combination with prefixes to form perfective verbs with an approximate meaning “to clothe, to dress, to put on”.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dęťi, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰengʰ-, *dʰn̥gʰ- (“to cover, conceal”). Cognate with Lithuanian deñgti (“to cover, to dress”).

parole.significato: Suffix appended to the nominal stem to create vocative singular. Used for masculine and neuter a-stems.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-e. Derived from Proto-Indo-European *-e, not a desinence per se but a thematic vowel in e-grade.

parole.significato: feminization suffix used to form a female equivalent used for wives
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-eva, from *-ovъ, from Proto-Indo-European *-us or *-os. Cognate with Polish -owa, the feminine of -owy. Compare Russian -ева (-eva), Slovincian -ôwo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ejь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьjь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ělь. An addition of *-lь to a stem extension *-ē. Reanalyzed as -е (-e) + -ль (-lʹ). Cognate Russian -ель (-elʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ělъ, from Proto-Indo-European *-éh₁ti + *-lós. With -ь m (-ʹ), parsable as Proto-Slavic *-ě- + Proto-Slavic *-lъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ěnъ, from Proto-Indo-European *-(e-)nós.

parole.significato: Used to form passive participles from imperfective and perfective verbs:
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -еный (-enyj), from Old East Slavic -енъ (-jenŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-jenъ.

parole.significato: Used to form passive participles from imperfective and perfective verbs:
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -еный (-enyj), from Old East Slavic -енъ (-jenŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-enъ.

parole.significato: Suffix used to form verbal nouns from verbs; added especially to verbs ending in -ити (-yty) (alternatively -їти (-jity…
parole.testo: Rebracketing of -ння (-nnja), from Proto-Slavic *-nьje. Compare Russian -ение (-enije), Belarusian -энне (-ennje), Polish -enie.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьnь. Compare Polish -eń.
Parsable as -ен- (-en-) + -я (-ja), by reduplication from Proto-Slavic *-ę.

parole.significato: Suffix appended to ordinal numerals to create a collective noun
parole.testo: From collective numerals suffix of Proto-Slavic *-er or *-or, which probably separated from stems of *četyr- /*četver- (*četvor-) /*četvьr- (чотири (čotyry)/четверо (četvero)/четвертий (četvertyj)) with further application to other numerals.

parole.significato: Suffix appended to imperfective verbs to create a masculine noun denoting result.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьtъ. Cognate with Russian -ет (-et).

parole.significato: Suffix appended to verbs to create a masculine noun denoting someone or something that performs the action denoted by t…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьcь.

parole.significato: Deadjectival suffix used to form abstract nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-eťa. Related to Serbo-Croatian -оћа.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ъkъ and *-ъka. Reanalyzed as -ьок (-ʹok) + -ок (-ok).

parole.significato: Combining form used to form imperfective counterparts of prefixed derivatives of зва́ти (zváty, “to call, to invite”).
parole.testo: From imperfective lengthening of the Proto-Slavic perfective infinitive stem *-zъv- (from the infinitive *zъvati) + -а́ти (-áty). Compare Russian -зыва́ть (-zyvátʹ), Belarusian -зыва́ць (-zyvácʹ).

parole.significato: Used form imperfective verbs with an approximate meaning “to look, to glance, to peek”.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zirati, the iterative of *zьrěti. Cognate with Russian -зирать (-ziratʹ), Polish -zierać, Old Church Slavonic -зирати (-zirati).

parole.significato: suffix appended to verbs to create nouns denoting act, state
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-znь. The spelling in the nominative case may have been influenced by Old Church Slavonic -знь (-znĭ), as -зень would probably be expected, compare Czech bázeň, Polish bojaźń, Serbo-Croatian бојазан, Slovene bojazen and Bulgarian боя́зън (bojázăn) exhibiting -zьnь while

parole.significato: Combining form used to form verbs meaning approximately "to shoe".
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uti.

parole.significato: -ia, a suffix used in place names.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьskъ.

parole.significato: Interfix used to form compound nouns and adjectives, when the first part is a verb or number.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-i-. Cognate with Polish -y-, Russian -и- (-i-).

parole.significato: -ful, -y, -ous (forms adjectives with the sense of "being characterized by the noun")
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -ивый (-ivyj), from Old East Slavic -ивъ (-ivŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ivъ.

parole.significato: deverbal suffix used to form nouns, that denote a product of the activity described by the verb
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -иво (-ivo), from Old East Slavic -иво (-ivo), from Proto-Slavic *-ivo. Compare Belarusian -іва (-iva).
Derived from Old Ruthenian -ий /-ый /-ій /-їй (-ij), from Proto-Slavic *-ъjь (/⁠*-ьjь /*-jьjь⁠/). Cognate with Belarusian -ы (-y), Russian -ый (-yj), Polish -y.

parole.significato: Suffix added to normally masculine nouns to form diminutives, sometimes with a further change in meaning.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ikъ.

parole.significato: Suffix appended to words to create a neuter noun, usually denoting senses or objects, used as an augmentative.
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *-dlo, appended to i-conjugation verbs. Rebracketing of -ло (-lo).

parole.significato: added to feminine nouns to form possessive adjectives, akin to English -'s
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic -инъ (-inŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-inъ, from Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos, from *-nós.

parole.significato: suffix appended to nouns to form concrete nouns having the quality of the original noun
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ina.

parole.significato: suffix used to form nouns denoting an event
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -ины (-iny), from Old East Slavic -ины (-iny), from Proto-Slavic *-iny, the plural of *-ina.

parole.significato: forms feminine equivalents of masculine animate nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-yni. By surface analysis, -ин (-yn) + -я (-ja). Compare Serbo-Croatian -иња, Pannonian Rusyn and Russian -иня (-inja), Polish -ini.

parole.significato: adjective-forming suffix, added to nouns, indicating having the property of that noun
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *-itъ / *-istъ. Compare Russian -истый (-istyj), Belarusian -ысты (-ysty) and -істы (-isty), Polish -ysty and -isty.

parole.significato: A suffix used to form verbs from nouns and adjectives.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-iti.

parole.significato: Forms nomina agentis from verbs or adjectives (rare)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ičь.

parole.significato: patronymic suffix added to a given name ending in a palatalized consonant
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic -ичь (-ičĭ), from Proto-Slavic *-iťь.

parole.significato: Аttached to nouns to form augmentatives.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-išče. Cognate Polish -yszcze, Bulgarian, Pannonian Rusyn, and Russian -ище (-išče).

parole.significato: Combining form used to form imperfective counterparts of prefixed derivatives of йня́ти (jnjáty) or -ня́ти (-njáty, “to…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьmati, whence also ма́ти (máty). Compare Belarusian -йма́ць (-jmácʹ), as well as archaic Russian има́ть (imátʹ), later reanalyzed as -нима́ть (-nimátʹ).

parole.significato: Suffix appended to words to create a feminine noun, denoting a part, profession, feature, membership, origin, social st…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ъka. Compare Swedish -ska.

parole.significato: -y, -ous: Used to form qualitative adjectives from verbs and nouns, with the meaning "having the characteristic of X".
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ъkъ. (*-ьkъ).

parole.significato: Creates diminutives of normally neuter nouns and adverbs, normally having a colloquial register.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьko.

parole.significato: -ful, -ly, -y, -ous, etc. (forms adjectives with the sense of "being characterized by the noun")
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -ливый (-livyj), from Old East Slavic -ливъ (-livŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-lъ + *-ivъ. By surface analysis, -л^((ий)) (-l⁽ʸʲ⁾) + -ивий (-yvyj) as rebracketing of -ивий (-yvyj). Cognate with Russian -ли́вый (-lívyj), Belarusian -лі́вы (-lívy), Polish -liwy.

parole.significato: used to form participle-like adjectives from intransitive verbs, usually the ones that describe state of being or chang…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-lъ.

parole.significato: -er (forms nouns denoting objects, generally tools or instruments, from verbs)
parole.testo: Ukrainian -лка In the meaning of a tool or instrument, may originate from a combination of tool suffix from Proto-Slavic *-dlo (Ukrainian -ло (-lo)) + the diminutive -ка (-ka). Cognate Belarusian, Bulgarian, Macedonian, and Russian -лка (-lka).

parole.significato: Suffix appended to verbs to create a neuter noun, normally denoting a tool.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-dlo, from Proto-Indo-European *-trom, from *-tḗr.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-lo. Cognate Polish -ło.

parole.significato: Unproductive deverbal suffix used to form nouns denoting a product or a result
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-lь, from *-lъ + *-ь. Cognate with Russian -ль (-lʹ).

parole.significato: Forms the present passive participle of imperfective verbs
Only used in conjunction with prefixes to form imperfective verbs with an approximate meaning "to pull (together), to l…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъčati.

parole.significato: Only used in conjunction with prefixes to form perfective verbs with an approximate meaning "to pull (together), to lin…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mъknǫti.

parole.significato: A feminine patronymic suffix added to a given name: daughter or wife of
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьna (feminine of *-ьnъ), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *-inas, from Proto-Indo-European *-nós. Compare Czech and Polish -na.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *na desęte. Compare Old Church Slavonic на десѧте (na desęte), Polish -naście, Russian -надцать (-nadcatʹ). By surface analysis, на (na) + десять (desjatʹ), literally “on ten”.

parole.significato: forms masculine agent nouns, denoting profession, occupation or relation;
parole.testo: Parallel to *-ьnica f for derivatives in feminine gender, inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьnikъ, itself originally by nominalization of adjectives in *-ьnъ with the suffix *-ikъ (whence -ик (-yk)). The suffix originates from the Proto-Balto-Slavic period; compare dialectal Lithuanian lauk-inykas (“pea
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьno. Cognate with Polish -no.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian -нꙋти (-nuti), from Old East Slavic -нꙋти (-nuti), from Proto-Slavic *-nǫti.

parole.significato: Used in combination with prefixes to form perfective verbs with an approximate meaning “to take”.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ęti (“to take”), reanalyzed as *nęti in verbs prefixed with *vъn-, *sъn- (*vъn-ęti → *vъ-nęti, *sъn-ęti → *sъ-nęti).

parole.significato: Combining form used to form imperfective counterparts of prefixed derivatives of -няти (-njaty, “to take”).
parole.testo: Based on reanalysis of the verbs зніма́ти (znimáty) as composed of з- (z-) plus a suffix -німа́ти. Originally -йма́ти (-jmáty) (cf. обійма́ти (obijmáty), прийма́ти (prijmáti)), from Proto-Slavic *jьmati (“to take”). See also -няти (-njaty).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian -о- (-o-), from Old East Slavic -о- (-o-), from Proto-Slavic *-o-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-oba.

parole.significato: Used to form relative adjectives from nouns; -y.
parole.testo: Derived from Old East Slavic -овъ (-ovŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ovъ, from Proto-Indo-European *-us or *-os.

parole.significato: -son, -s, (relational) suffix used in many surnames and placenames, predominately from Russian
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic -овъ (-ovŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ovъ. Reanalyzed as -ов (-ov) + -о (-o).

parole.significato: takes masculine nouns, produces diminutive masculine nouns, sometimes with further sense development
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ъkъ, from *-kъ, from Proto-Indo-European *-kos.

parole.significato: _(non-ar/-j) instrumental singular of -∅ (zero suffix, indicates the hard-stem nouns' nominative singular of masculine…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -омъ (-om), from Old East Slavic -ъмь (-ŭmĭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ъmь, the instrumental ending of o-stem and u-stem nouns. Compare Upper Sorbian -om, Bulgarian, Russian -ом (-om).

parole.significato: an obsolete suffix originally used to form present passive participles, which can be found as a fossil in a few former…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -омый (-omyj), from Old East Slavic -омъ (-omŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-omъ, a present passive participle suffix.

parole.significato: Suffix appended to nouns to create a collective noun
parole.testo: From collective numerals suffix of Proto-Slavic *-er or *-or, which probably separated from stems of *četyr- /*četver- (*četvor-) /*četvьr- (чотири (čotyry)/четверо (četvero)/четвертий (četvertyj)) with further application to other numerals.

parole.significato: Suffix appended to words to create a feminine noun, usually an abstract noun denoting a quality.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ota.
Originally a double diminutive Proto-Slavic *-ъčьka formed from *-ъka + *-ьka. Reanalyzed as -ка (-ka) + -ка (-ka).

parole.significato: -ness (deadjectival nominalizing suffix used to create nouns, that denote quality or state);
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic -ощи (-ošči), from hypothetical Proto-Slavic *-ošča, from *-ostь + *-ja. Words featuring this suffix were originally used in insturmental plural and functioned as adverbs: Old East Slavic жалощами (žaloščami, “pitifully, mournfully”), радощами (radoščami, “happily, gla

parole.significato: Combining form used to form imperfective counterparts of prefixed derivatives of слати (slaty, “to send”).
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъlati.
From the Proto-Slavic *-slavъ ending in names such as *Voldislavъ, from Proto-Slavic *slava (“glory, fame”).

parole.significato: Suffix added to nouns and adjectives to create an abstract noun, corresponding to English -ness, -hood, -dom.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьstvo, from Proto-Indo-European *-tus.

parole.significato: Used with past plural forms of imperfective (rarely perfective) verbs, marking them as second-person plural.
parole.testo: Contraction of Proto-Slavic *este, second-person plural of *byti. Previously marked the perfect aspect, as in Old Church Slavonic. Cognate with Polish -ście, which is also used with former l-participles to form the past tense.

parole.significato: Appended to relative/interrogative pronouns to form indefinite pronouns: some-
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic си (si), from Proto-Slavic *si. Compare synonymous Russian -то (-to) ultimately from *tъ (“that”), similar Polish -ś.

parole.significato: this, last (found in a few, mostly obsolete or dialectal, terms referring to time)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sь (“this”). Doublet of цей (cej), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic. Cognates Belarusian and Russian -сь (-sʹ). See also сей (sej), the inherited independent form.

parole.significato: -ia, a suffix used in place names.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьskъ.

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives, often from nouns; -ish, -y, of -'s (double genitive).
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -ский (-skij), from Old East Slavic -ьскъ (-ĭskŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ьskъ. Cognate with Russian -ский (-skij), Belarusian -скі (-ski), Polish -ski, Czech -ský.

parole.significato: Reflexive suffix appended to finite verbs and infinitives to make a reflexive, reciprocal, intransitive or passive verb.
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic сѧ (sę), from Proto-Slavic *sę, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *sen, from Proto-Indo-European *swé.

parole.significato: Unproductive denominal and deverbal, forms feminine nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьta (feminine of *-ьtъ).

parole.significato: forms deverbal abstract nouns denoting an act, state or result
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -тва (-tva), from Old East Slavic -тва (-tva), from Proto-Slavic *-tva.

parole.significato: appended to verbs and nouns to form masculine agent nouns; -er, -or
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -тель (-telʹ), from Old East Slavic -тель (-telĭ), from Proto-Slavic *-teľь.

parole.significato: The infinitive ending of verbs in Ukrainian.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ti.

parole.significato: Deverbal from perfective mono-syllabic simple stems, forms passive participles
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-tъ. From Proto-Balto-Slavic *-tas; the suffix continues both Proto-Indo-European *-tós and *-tus. For the participle use, compare Proto-Germanic *-þaz and Latin -tus. However the verb classes that take *-þaz in Proto-Germanic (so-called “weak verbs”) take *-nъ (“-ний”)

parole.significato: -ion, -ence, -ance, -ity, etc. (suffix used to form abstract nouns from verbs)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -тѧ, -тє (-tja, -tje), from Old East Slavic -тьѥ (-tĭje), from Proto-Slavic *-tьje.

parole.significato: used in combination with prefixes to form perfective verbs with an approximate meaning “to tense, to strain”.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tǫžiti. By surface analysis, туги́й (tuhýj) + -ити (-yty).

parole.significato: Alternative infinitive ending, often used poetically.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ti, through the variant *-tь.

parole.significato: Forms verbs from nouns and adjectives, as well as loanwords.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ovati. Compare Macedonian -ува (-uva), Polish -ować.

parole.significato: forms feminine nouns of both animacies
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-uga. Compare Polish -uga, Russian -у́га (-úga).

parole.significato: Added to an often diminutive stem to form a patronymic or matronymic surname
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ukъ.

parole.significato: Suffix appended to verbs to create a masculine noun, normally denoting an actor.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-unъ. Compare Polish -un, Russian -ун (-un).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-unь. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(∅)-ḗn. Compare Polish -uń.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-urъ.

parole.significato: -ure, -cy; appended to nouns to form feminine inanimate abstract nouns, often collective in meaning
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ura. Compare Bulgarian and Russian -ура (-ura), Polish -ura.

parole.significato: used with an adjective, noun, participle or verb to form a masculine agent noun that is often augmentative
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-uxъ. Compare Russian -ух (-ux), Polish -uch.

parole.significato: Adjective-forming suffix, added to intransitive verbs, indicating being in the state of that verb.

parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-xа (feminine of *-xъ). Morphologicaly augmentative of -шка (-ška). Compare Russian -а́ха (-áxa).

parole.significato: Combining form used to form prefixed perfective verbs with the approximate meaning of "to choke".

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьce, from Proto-Indo-European *-ikos.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьskъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *-iškas, from Proto-Indo-European *-iskos.

parole.significato: Suffix appended to words to create a feminine noun, usually a diminutive form expressing endearment.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьca, from *-ьka, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *-ikāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *-i-keh₂, from *-keh₂.

parole.significato: Only used in conjunction with prefixes to form perfective verbs with an approximate meaning "to survive, to stay intact…

Derived from Proto-Slavic *-ьšь (comparative suffix). Used to form the comparative degree of adjectives.

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -шний (-šnij), from Old East Slavic -чьнии, -шьнии (-čĭnii, -šĭnii), from Proto-Slavic *-ťь + *-ьňь or extracted from Proto-Slavic *domaťьňь. Parsable as -ш (-š) + -ній (-nij).

parole.significato: forms nouns denoting objects or (usually) abstract concepts from verbs, or occasionally from adjectives
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ь. Via Old East Slavic -ь (-ĭ).

parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-jь (/⁠Suffix 2⁠/), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *-jas, from Proto-Indo-European *-yós. Via Old East Slavic -и (-i).

parole.significato: -ing (deverbal suffix used to form action nouns)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -ьба (-ʹba), from Old East Slavic -ьба (-ĭba), from Proto-Slavic *-ьba.

parole.significato: Added to a stem to form a patronymic or matronymic surname
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ukъ.

parole.significato: Appended to nouns to form inanimate nouns often augmentative in meaning
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ura. Compare Polish -ura.

parole.significato: Noun-forming diminutive suffix used after a soft (palatalized) consonant.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ja. Cognate Russian -я (-ja).

parole.significato: Forms nouns for young animals and other diminutives.

parole.significato: Suffix used to form adjectives from nouns or other adjectives, usually describing characteristics; approximately equiva…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-(a)vъ.

parole.significato: adjective-forming suffix, added to nouns, indicating being composed of or related to that noun; normally forms relation…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ěnъ, from Proto-Indo-European *-(e-)nós. Compare Russian -я́ный (-jányj), -яно́й (-janój).

parole.significato: Suffix used to form nouns from other nouns, usually referring to inhabitants of a given place or occupations.
parole.testo: Reanalyzed as -ян (-jan) + -ин (-yn).

parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *-atъ / *-аstъ. Compare Russian -астый (-astyj), Belarusian -асты (-asty). Reanalyze as -яст (-jast) + -ий (-yj)

used to form present active participles from class 4 verbs (in -ити (-yty)) and from class 5 verbs (in -іти (-ity), -ят…

parole.significato: -son, -s, (relational) suffix used in many surnames and placenames, predominately from Russian
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic -овъ (-ovŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ovъ. By surface analysis, -єв (-jev) + -о (-o)

parole.significato: Suffix appended to verbs to create a masculine noun denoting someone or something that performs the action denoted by t…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьcь.

parole.significato: Forms possessive adjectives of hard-, velar-, soft-, and semisoft-stem personal masculine nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -овъ (-ov), from Old East Slavic -овъ (-ovŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ovъ. Doublet of -ов (-ov).

parole.significato: suffix used to form verbal nouns that usually denote the result of the action
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian -ежъ, -ѣжъ (-ež, -ěž), from Old East Slavic -ежь (-ježĭ), from Proto-Slavic *-ežь.

parole.significato: appended to verbs to form masculine agent nouns; -er, -or, -ist

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ělь. Reanalyzed as -і (-i) + -ль f (-lʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ělъ.

parole.significato: -tion, -ence, -ance, -ity, etc. (suffix used to form abstract nouns from verbs, and occasionally from other parts of sp…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-nьje. Rebracketing of -ння (-nnja).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-nь.

parole.significato: Suffix appended to imperfective verbs to create a masculine noun denoting action.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-otъ.

parole.significato: Suffix added to adjectives to form intransitive verbs that describe having or gaining the property of said adjective.

Inherited from Old East Slavic -инъ (-inŭ), from Proto-Slavic *-inъ. See also -ин (-yn).

parole.significato: suffix appended to nouns to form concrete nouns having the quality of the original noun
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ina f.

parole.significato: forms feminine equivalents of masculine animate nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-yni. By surface analysis, -їн (-jin) + -я (-ja). Compare Polish -yni.

From Old Ruthenian або (abo), from Old East Slavic або (abo), from Proto-Slavic *abo.

parole.significato: sum of overground parts of certain plant cultures
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *badylьje, the collective of *badylь.

parole.significato: to desire, to want, to wish
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bažati (“to desire, to crave”). Cognate to Belarusian бажа́ць (bažácʹ), Czech bažit, Russian бажи́ть (bažítʹ). Compare the names of Old East Slavic origin: Бажéн (Bažén) and Бажéна (Bažéna), from Proto-Slavic *baženъ (“desired”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bajьka.

parole.significato: to speak, to talk, to chatter
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian бала́кати (balákati), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *balàkati. Cognate with Belarusian бала́каць (balákacʹ), Russian бала́кать (balákatʹ).

Variously explained, most likely ultimately from Proto-Slavic *bal- (“conversation, chatter”) + *mǫt- (“trouble, disorder”). Attested as (VIth) century баламутъ (balamut, “desolate man, windbreaker”). Cognate with Polish bałamut, Czech balamuta (“chaos, confusion, spreading of gossip”), Slovene bala
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *balъka.

parole.significato: to spoil, to indulge, to pamper, to cosset
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic баловати (balovati, “to treat, to heal”), from Proto-Slavic *badlovati. Cognate with Belarusian ба́лаваць (bálavacʹ), Russian балова́ть (balovátʹ), Old Church Slavonic баловати (balovati).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *baňa.

From ба́ня (bánja) + -я́к (-ják), from Old East Slavic банꙗ (banja, “bathing place”) from Proto-Slavic *baňa, from Vulgar Latin *bānea, from Latin balneum, from Ancient Greek βαλανεῖον (balaneîon, “bath, bathhouse”).
From Old East Slavic баранъ (baranŭ), from Proto-Slavic *baranъ.

parole.significato: to detain, to keep, to stop (somebody)

From Proto-Slavic *bьrlogъ.

From Old Ruthenian бато́гъ (batóh), from Old East Slavic бато́гъ (batógŭ), from Proto-Slavic *batogъ.

parole.significato: to speak, to tell (also used in folklore)

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bъgati.

From Proto-Slavic *bъlzьnь.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bezumьnъ. By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + ум (um, “mind”) + -ний (-nyj). Compare Russian безу́мный (bezúmnyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bezimenьnъ. By surface analysis, без- (bez-) + імен- (imen-, stem of ім'я́ (imʺjá)) + -ний (-nyj).

From Proto-Slavic *besěda. Cognate with Bulgarian беседа (beseda), Czech beseda.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bičь.

parole.significato: to whip, to lash, to scourge, to flog
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian бичова́ти, бичева́ти (bičováti, bičeváti, “to whip, to lash”), from Proto-Slavic *bičevati. By surface analysis, бич (byč) + -увати (-uvaty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bolgo.

From Old East Slavic бльвати (blĭvati), from Proto-Slavic *bľьvati (“to vomit”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *blědъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian бо (bo), from Old East Slavic бо (bo), from Proto-Slavic *bo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bobrъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian болва́нъ (bolván), from Old East Slavic бълванъ (bŭlvanŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bъlvanъ. Doublet of болва́н (bolván), from Russian болва́н (bolván).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bьltati.

parole.significato: cheerful, brisk, lively, energetic, sprightly, hale
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian бо́дрый (bódryj), from Old East Slavic бъдръ (bŭdrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bъdrъ. The reemergence of бо́дрий (bódryj) in modern colloquial Ukrainian most likely occurred under the influence of Russian бо́дрый (bódryj). Doublet of бадьо́рий (badʹóryj).

parole.significato: to swear to God, to swear on a stack of Bibles, to swear, to oath
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian божи́тисѧ (božítisja), from Old East Slavic божитисꙗ (božitisja), from Proto-Slavic *božiti. By surface analysis, бог (boh) + -ити (-yty) + -ся (-sja).
Inherited from Old East Slavic божьница (božĭnica), from Proto-Slavic *božьnica, from *božьnъ + *-ica or *bogъ + *-ьnica. Equivalent to бог (boh) + -ни́ця (-nýcja).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bojevъ. Analyzable as бій (bij) + -ови́й (-ovýj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bolto.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian болѣсть, болесть (bolěstʹ, bolestʹ), from Old East Slavic болесть, болѥсть (bolestĭ, boljestĭ), from Proto-Slavic *bolestь or *boľestь. By surface analysis, біль m (bilʹ) + -есть (-estʹ).

parole.significato: to be sick, to be ill, to be ailing
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bolěti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic борьць (borĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *borьcь, from *borti + *-ьcь. By surface analysis, бор(о́ти) (bor(óty)) + -е́ць (-écʹ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic бързъ (bŭrzŭ), from Proto-Slavic *bъrzъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bъrkati.
From Proto-Slavic *bordà, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bardā́ˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰéh₂.

parole.significato: wart (type of growth occurring on the skin)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bordavъka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bordàtъ. By surface analysis, борода́ (borodá) + -а́тий (-átyj).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian борозна́ (borozná), from Old East Slavic борозда (borozda), from Proto-Slavic *borzda.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian борона (borona), from Proto-Slavic *borna. Cognate with Belarusian барана́ (baraná). Doublet of бра́ма (bráma, “gate”), a borrowing from Polish.

parole.significato: to protect, to defend, to safeguard
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian борони́ти (boroníti), from Old East Slavic боронити (boroniti), from Proto-Slavic *borniti.

parole.significato: to be winning in a fight, to overcome
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic бороти (boroti, “to fight”), from Proto-Slavic *borti.

боро́тися (borótysja) + -ьба́ (-ʹbá). Likely a later reformation, other languages mostly reflect Proto-Slavic *borьba (whence also dialectal Ukrainian борба́ (borbá)). Cognate with Belarusian барацьба́ (baracʹbá).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *boršьno.

parole.significato: to flounder, to flail, to flail about, to struggle, to thrash about
parole.testo: Uncertain. Oleg Trubachyov suggests a connection with Proto-Slavic *brъsati / *brъsiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bъrščь, first meaning “hogweed”, then “hogweed soup”, later “beet soup”, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *bursktis. For the semantic shift compare Polish barszcz.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bosъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bosonogъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bъčьka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bojaznь. By surface analysis, боя́тися (bojátysja) + -знь (-znʹ)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bojati sę.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian бра́га (bráha), from Proto-Slavic *braga.
From Proto-Slavic *bratrъ, *bratъ.

parole.testo: From Old East Slavic бьрати (bĭrati), from Proto-Slavic *bьrati. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.

parole.significato: brotherhood, fraternity, brethren (an association of people)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bratrьstvo. By surface analysis, брат (brat, “brother”) + -ство (-stvo). Doublet of брате́рство (bratérstvo).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bràtьskъ. By surface analysis, брат (brat, “brother”) + -ський (-sʹkyj).

parole.significato: to plod, to slog, to trudge, to lumber
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian брести́ (brestí), from Old East Slavic брести (bresti), from Proto-Slavic *bresti.
From Proto-Slavic *brexati, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerk-, from *bʰer-. Cognate with Belarusian брахаць (braxacʹ), Russian брехать (brexatʹ), Slovak brechat'.
From Proto-Slavic *brexati, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerk-, from *bʰer-. Cognate with Belarusian брахаць (braxacʹ), Russian брехать (brexatʹ), Slovak brechat'.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bridъkъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bryzgati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bryzgnǫti.

parole.significato: to kick by the hind legs (horse, bovine etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brъkati.

parole.significato: block, clod, clump, hunk, lump (unshaped solid mass)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bryla. Compare Polish bryła.

parole.significato: to jingle, to clink, to chink
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bręčati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brъněti.
From Proto-Slavic *britva, from *briti + *-tva. By surface analysis, брити (bryty) + -тва (-tva).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brìti.
From Old East Slavic бръвь (brŭvĭ), from Proto-Slavic *bry.
Inherited from Old East Slavic бродити (broditi), from Proto-Slavic *brodìti, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrodʰ-eye-, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰredʰ-.
Inherited from Old East Slavic брънꙗ (brŭnja), from Proto-Slavic *brъňa, from Gothic 𐌱𐍂𐌿𐌽𐌾𐍉 (brunjō, “breastplate”), from Proto-Germanic *brunjǭ (“breastplate”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brudъ.

parole.significato: a balk (squared or squared-off beam or timber)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brusъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brusьnica.
From Proto-Slavic *brusъkъ (“hone, whetstone”), from Proto-Slavic *brusъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bręknǫti (“to swell”), with -нути (-nuty)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brodъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bǫbьniti. By surface analysis, бу́бон (búbon, “tambourine”) + -і́ти (-íty). Doublet of бубні́ти (bubníty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bugrъ.

parole.significato: to wake up, to awaken, to waken, to wake
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian буди́ти (budíti), from Old East Slavic будити (buditi), from Proto-Slavic *buditi.
From earlier буз (buz), боз (boz), from Proto-Slavic *bъzъ (“elder”), the sense “lilac” bearing now the standard form бузо́к (buzók). With -ина (-yna)
From earlier буз (buz), боз (boz), from Proto-Slavic *bъzъ (“elder”), the sense “elder” bearing now the standard form бузина́ (buzyná).

parole.significato: stormy, raging, violent (involving extreme force or motion)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bujьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bukъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic бꙋкꙑ (buky), from Proto-Slavic *buky.
Compare Slovak burina and Romanian buruiană, from Proto-Slavic *burьjanъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *buřelomъ.

parole.significato: to mumble, to murmur, to mutter
parole.testo: Onomatopoeic, possibly inherited from Proto-Slavic *bъrmotati. Compare Russian бормота́ть (bormotátʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *buřa.

From Old East Slavic бꙑти (byti), from Proto-Slavic *byti. The u in the infinitive and past tense was probably influenced by the future tense. Compare Pannonian Rusyn буц (buc) as well as (rare and possibly hyper-corrected) Old Novgorodian буть (butĭ) for the infinitive and Belarusian быць (bycʹ) fo

Inherited from Old East Slavic бꙑтие (bytije), from Proto-Slavic *bytьje. Analyzable as бу́ти impf (búty, “to be”) + -я (-ja). Compare Russian бытие́ (bytijé), Belarusian быццё (byccjó), Polish bycie.

parole.significato: to thud, to thump, to flump, to bang, to boom (to produce a dull, heavy, abrupt sound, the sound of a blunt impact)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *buxati, of onomatopoeic origin. By surface analysis, бух (bux) + -ати (-aty).

parole.significato: to flourish, to proliferate, to develop rapidly
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bujati.
Inherited from Middle Ukrainian бѡбъ (bôb), from бобъ (bob), from Proto-Slavic *bobъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *běgъ. Doublet of Фоб (Fob).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *běgati.

The infinitive and past tense forms come from Old Ruthenian бѣчи (běči), while the present tense forms come from Old Ruthenian бѣжати (běžati), from Old East Slavic бѣчи, бѣжати (běči, běžati), from Proto-Slavic *běťi and *běžati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *běgunъ. Equivalent to бігати (bihaty) + -ун (-un).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *běda.
From Proto-Slavic *bědьnъ. Morphologically, from біда́ (bidá) + -ний (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bědьňakъ. By surface analysis, бі́дний (bídnyj) + -я́к (-ják). Compare Russian бедня́к (bednják), Belarusian бядня́к (bjadnják).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bojь, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoyh₂ós, from *bʰeyh₂- (“to strike, hew”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bokъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bělъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian бѣли́ти (bělíti), from Old East Slavic бѣлити (běliti), from Proto-Slavic *běliti. By surface analysis, біл (bil) + -ити (-yty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bolь.
From Proto-Slavic *boľьjь + -ше (-še).

From early піля (pilja) < *підля (*pidlja) < *пюдлѧ (*pjudlja) < *пѡдлѣ (*pôdli), from Old Ruthenian подлѣ (podlě, “near”), from Old East Slavic подьлѣ (podĭlě, “by length”), ultimately from по (po) + дьлѣ (dĭlě), prefixed variant of Proto-Slavic *dьlь (“length”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *bělěti. By surface analysis, бі́лий (bílyj) + -і́ти (-íty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian боръ m (bor), буръ m (bur), from Proto-Slavic *bȍrъ m, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *barús m, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰor- (“coniferous forest”). Cognate with Belarusian бор m (bor), Polish bór m, Bulgarian бор m (bor), etc.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *běsъ.

parole.significato: to madden, to piss off, to vex, to irritate, to annoy
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian *бѣсити (*běsiti) (att. in бѣситиcѧ (běsiticja)), from Proto-Slavic *běsiti. By surface analysis, біс (bis) + -и́ти (-ýty).

parole.significato: in, at [with locative] (used to express static position/location; followed by a vowel)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic въ (vŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vъ(n), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁n̥, zero-grade form of *h₁én.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vę̄zàti.

parole.significato: to bog (down), to stick, to get stuck, to sink (in mud, snow etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian вѧзнꙋти (vjaznuti), from Old East Slavic вѧзнꙋти (vęznuti), from Proto-Slavic *vęznǫti. By surface analysis, в'яза́ти (vʺjazáty) + -нути (-nuty).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian вѧнути (vjanuti), from Old East Slavic вѧнѫти (vęnǫti), from Proto-Slavic *vędnǫti, with -нути (-nuty). Akin to German schwinden.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian в-, въ- (v-, v-), from Old East Slavic въ- (vŭ-), from Proto-Slavic *vъ(n)-.

parole.significato: to attract, to draw, to tempt
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian вабити (vabiti), from Old East Slavic вабити (vabiti), from Proto-Slavic *vabiti. Cognate to Belarusian ва́біць (vábicʹ), Czech vábit, Polish wabić, Bulgarian ва́бя (vábja).

parole.significato: to hinder, to obstruct, to hamper, to be in the way (with dative)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vaditi. The primary meaning is likely a semantic loan from Polish wadzić (“to hinder, to obstruct”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic валъ (valŭ), from Proto-Slavic *valъ

parole.significato: to topple, to bring down, to knock down
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian вали́ти (valíti), from Old East Slavic валити (valiti), from Proto-Slavic *valiti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic вапьно (vapĭno), from Proto-Slavic *vapьno.
Inherited from Old East Slavic вапьно (vapĭno), from Proto-Slavic *vapьno. Compare Belarusian ва́пна (vápna), Serbo-Croatian вапно́, Czech vápno, Slovak vápno, Polish wapno.
From Proto-Slavic *variti, from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to burn”).

parole.significato: your, yours (2nd-person singular formal or 2nd-person plural)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *vašь, from Proto-Indo-European *wōsyo-.

parole.significato: to hit, to strike, to smite (to deal a blow)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian уда́рити, вда́рити (udáriti, vdáriti), from Old East Slavic оударити (udariti), from Proto-Slavic *udariti, from Proto-Indo-European *derH-.
From Proto-Slavic *vьdova, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *widewāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂.
Univerbation of в (v) + *до́сталь (*dóstalʹ), from Proto-Slavic *dostati.
By metathesis from Proto-Slavic *medvědь.

parole.significato: to carry (by vehicle), to transport, to haul

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *velikъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *veličina. By surface analysis, вели́кий (velýkyj) + -ина́ (-yná).
Inherited from Old East Slavic велѣти (velěti), from Proto-Slavic *velěti. Cognate with Russian велеть (veletʹ), Old Church Slavonic велѣти (velěti), Serbo-Croatian вѐлӣм, Czech velet.
From Old East Slavic вепрь (veprĭ), from Proto-Slavic *veprь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vьrba.
From Proto-Slavic *velьb(l)ǫdъ, *vъlьb(l)ǫdъ.

parole.significato: one of the ropes on which a baby cradle is suspended
parole.testo: Derived from Old East Slavic вьрвь (vĭrvĭ), from Proto-Slavic *vьrvь (deverbal of *verti), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to tie, string; rope”) which is ultimately cognate with *wer- (“to turn, bend”) whence the two meanings of the verb. Compare Russian верёвка (verjóvka), whence Ukrainian вірьо́
Inherited from Middle Ukrainian вервица (vervyca), from Old East Slavic вьрвь (vĭrvĭ), from Proto-Slavic *vьrvь, with diminutive ending -иця (-ycja). Compare Russian ве́рвица (vérvica).

parole.significato: to cast, to toss, to throw, to fling, to lob

parole.significato: to cast, to toss, to throw, to fling, to lob
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ве́ргнути (vérhnuti), from Old East Slavic вьргнꙋти (vĭrgnuti), from Proto-Slavic *vьrgnǫti.

parole.significato: to cast, to toss, to throw, to fling, to lob
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian вергти (verhti), from Proto-Slavic *vьrťi.
Inherited from Old East Slavic вередъ (veredŭ), inherited from Proto-Slavic *verdъ. Doublet of вред (vred), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian вереди́ти (veredíti), from Old East Slavic вередити (verediti), from Proto-Slavic *verditi. By surface analysis, веред (vered) + -и́ти (-ýty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian веремѧ (veremja, “time”), from Proto-Slavic *vermę. Compare Bulgarian вре́ме (vréme), Macedonian вре́ме (vréme), Slovene vréme. Doublet of вре́м'я (vrémʺja), borrowed from Church Slavonic.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian верескъ (veresk), from Old East Slavic верескъ (vereskŭ), from Proto-Slavic *verskъ. Cognate with Belarusian ве́раск (vjérask), Polish wrzask, Czech vřesk, Serbo-Croatian ври̑сак.
From Old East Slavic веретено (vereteno), from Proto-Slavic *verteno (“spindle”).

parole.significato: to squeal (to scream a high-pitched squeal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian вереща́ти (vereščáti), from Proto-Slavic *verščati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vьrzti.

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian верну́ти (vernúti), from Proto-Slavic *vьrtnǫti, *vьrnǫti. By surface analysis, вер- (ver-) + -нути (-nuty).

parole.significato: verst (former unit of length, equal to 1.06 kilometers)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic вьрста (vĭrsta), from Proto-Slavic *vьrsta. Cognate with Russian верста́ (verstá), Old East Slavic вьрста (vĭrsta, “age, couple, age-mate, verst (measure of length)”), Old Church Slavonic врьста (vrĭsta, “age”), Bulgarian връст (vrăst, “age”), Serbo-Croatian вр́ста (“r
From Proto-Slavic *vьrstva, ultimately from the same source as Etymology 1. Cognate with Polish warstwa.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian верта́ти (vertáti), from Proto-Slavic *vьrtati.
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *vьrtъpъ.

parole.significato: to do, to complete, to accomplish, to carry out
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian верши́ти (veršíti), from Old East Slavic вьршити (vĭršiti), from Proto-Slavic *vьršiti. By surface analysis, верх (verx) + -и́ти (-ýty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *veselъ.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian веселити (veseliti), from Old East Slavic веселити (veseliti), from Proto-Slavic *veseliti. By surface analysis, весе́л(ий) (vesél(yj)) + -и́ти (-ýty). Compare Russian весели́ть (veselítʹ), Belarusian весялі́ць (vjesjalícʹ), Polish weselić.
Inherited from Middle Ukrainian весло (veslo), from Old East Slavic весло (veslo), from Proto-Slavic *veslo (“oar”).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vьśь. Cognate with Sanskrit विश्व (viśva, “all”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vьsь.

Compare Polish wesele, Belarusian вяселле (vjasjellje), Slovak veselie, all meaning "wedding party", Romanian veselie (“joy”). By surface analysis, веселий (veselyj, “happy, merry”) + -я (-ja). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *veselьje either directly or via Polish.
From Old East Slavic ветъхъ (vetŭxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vetъxъ (“old, ancient”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *večeřa.

parole.significato: to have dinner, to have supper
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *večeřati.
From Proto-Slavic *večerъ, from Proto-Indo-European *wekʷsperos.

Proto-Slavic *vъz-, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *uź-. Cognate with Lithuanian už (“within, instead of, in return for”), Latvian uz (“on, to”). Further etymology disputed. Compare also воз- (voz-), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vъzajьmьnъ.
From взає́мний (vzajémnyj) + -о- (-o-), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *vъzajьmьnъ. Cognate with Russian взаимо- (vzaimo-).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vъzęti. By surface analysis, вз- (vz-) + Proto-Slavic *ęti

parole.significato: Second-person singular formal pronoun used in documents e.g. applications, reports, legal papers, etc.
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic вы (vy), from Proto-Slavic *vy.
From Old East Slavic вы (vy), from Proto-Slavic *vy.

parole.significato: out, ex- (describing an action of moving outside from inside)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian вы- (vy-), from Old East Slavic вꙑ- (vy-), from Proto-Slavic *vy-.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian вѣверка (věverka), from Proto-Slavic *věverъka.
From Old East Slavic видъ (vidŭ), from Proto-Slavic *vidъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wéiˀdas, from Proto-Indo-European *wéydos, from *weyd-.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian выдавати (vydavati), from Old East Slavic вꙑдавати (vydavati), from Proto-Slavic *vydavati. By surface analysis, ви- (vy-) + дава́ти (daváty).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian *выдати (*vydati), from Old East Slavic вꙑдати (vydati), from Proto-Slavic *vydati. By surface analysis, ви́- (vý-) + да́ти (dáty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vidati or *viďati. Compare Russian вида́ть (vidátʹ), Polish widać.

parole.significato: whirlwind, vortex (of wind or windborne objects)

parole.significato: wool (hair of sheep and some other ruminants)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic вълна (vŭlna, “wool”), Proto-Slavic *vьlna (“wool”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *wílˀnāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wĺ̥h₁neh₂ (“wool”).

parole.significato: to own, to possess, to have, to be in possession of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian воло́дати (volódati), from Proto-Slavic *voldati. Doublet of влада́ти (vladáty).

parole.significato: to own, to possess, to be master of, to be in possession of
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *volděti (“to rule”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *walˀdā́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁dʰh₁-, from *h₂welh₁- (“to rule”).

parole.significato: to moisten, to moisturize, to wet

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *volkъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *grozьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gromъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěnъka, *grěnъkъ, from Proto-Slavic *grěti (“to heat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm”).

parole.significato: to give off warmth, to give off heat
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěti, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěxъ.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian грѣхо́вный (hrěxóvnyj), from Old East Slavic грѣховьнъ (grěxovĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *grěxovьnъ. Compare Russian грехо́вный (grexóvnyj). By surface analysis, гріх (hrix) + -овний (-ovnyj).
From Proto-Slavic *grěšiti, also analysable as гріх (hrix) + -ити (-yty).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gǫba. Doublet of ґе́мба (gémba), which was borrowed from Polish.

parole.significato: to lose (cause to cease to be in one's possession or capability due to unfortunate or unknown circumstances, events or…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gubiti.

parole.significato: sponge (any of various marine invertebrates of the phylum Porifera)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gǫbъka, from *gǫba + *-ъka. By surface analysis, гу́ба (húba) + -ка (-ka). Compare Polish gąbka (“sponge”) and Polish hubka (“amadou”).

parole.significato: to condemn, to reprimand, to reproach, to criticize
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian гꙋдити (huditi), from Old East Slavic гꙋдити (guditi), from Proto-Slavic *guditi. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic гоудити (guditi).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian гудьба (hudʹba), from Old East Slavic гꙋдьба (gudĭba), from Proto-Slavic *gǫdьba.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gukъ. Cognate with Belarusian гук (huk), Polish huk.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gukati. By surface analysis, гук (huk) + ати (aty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gǫsakъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ǫsěnica.
From archaic or dialectal гусь (husʹ, “goose”) + -еня́ (-enjá), from Proto-Slavic *gǫ̑sь.
Plural of archaic or dialectal гусь (husʹ, “goose”), from Proto-Slavic *gǫ̑sь.
From Proto-Slavic *gǫ̑sь, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns.
From Old East Slavic гоусли (gusli), from Proto-Slavic *gǫsli.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gǫsti. Cognate with Old Polish gąść and Belarusian гусці́ (huscí).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gǫstъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gǫstiti, from *gǫ̑stъ + *-iti. By surface analysis, густи́й (hustýj) + -и́ти (-ýty). Compare Russian густи́ть (gustítʹ), Polish gęścić.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gǫ̑sь.
From archaic or dialectal гусь (husʹ, “goose”) + -я́ (-já), from Proto-Slavic *gǫ̑sь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *govьno.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *godьnъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian гольє, голє (holʹje, holje), from Proto-Slavic *golьje. By surface analysis, голий (holyj) + -я (-ja).
From Old East Slavic говьно (govĭno), from Proto-Slavic *govьno.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gorьkъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gorьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gorьčica. By surface analysis, гірки́й (hirkýj, “bitter”) + -и́ця (-ýcja).
From Middle Ukrainian гость (hostʹ), from Old East Slavic гость (gostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *gostь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gastís, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis.
Inherited from Old East Slavic да (da), from Proto-Slavic *da.
From Proto-Slavic *dāvàti. Composed as if from да́ти (dáty) + -ва́ти (-váty).

Inherited from Old East Slavic дави́ти (davíti), from Proto-Slavic *daviti. Cognate with Belarusian даві́ць (davícʹ), Russian дави́ть (davítʹ), Czech dávit, Polish dawić, Bulgarian да́вя (dávja), Serbo-Croatian да́вити.

parole.significato: ancient times, antiquity, days of old, olden times
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *davьnina. By surface analysis, да́вній (dávnij) + -ина́ (-yná).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *davьnъ. Doublet of дре́вній (drévnij).

parole.significato: far, distant, remote (but, to express 'to be far from', далеко + від must be used instead)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dalekъ. By surface analysis, даль (dalʹ) + -кий (-kyj).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian дани́на (danína), from Proto-Slavic *danina. By surface analysis, да́ний (dányj) + -ина (-yna).
From Old East Slavic дань (danĭ), from Proto-Slavic *danь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dṓˀnis, from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃-.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian даръ (dar), from Old East Slavic даръ (darŭ), from Proto-Slavic *darъ.

parole.significato: to gift, to give, to bestow, to donate, to present (something to someone: кому́сь (dative) щось (accusative))
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian дари́ти (daríti), from Old East Slavic дарити (dariti), from Proto-Slavic *dariti. Equivalent to дар (dar) + -ити (-yty). Cognate with Belarusian дары́ць (darýcʹ), Russian дари́ть (darítʹ), Czech dařit, Polish darzyć.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian дармо, дарма (darmo, darma), from Proto-Slavic *darьmo. Doublet of да́рмо (dármo).

parole.significato: to gift, to give, to bestow, to donate, to present (something to someone: кому́сь (dative) щось (accusative))
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *darovati. By surface analysis, дар (dar) + -ува́ти (-uváty).
From Proto-Slavic *dati, Proto-Balto-Slavic *dṓˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti (“to give”).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian датокъ (datok), from Proto-Slavic *datъkъ. By surface analysis, дати (daty) + -ок (-ok).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъva.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъva desęti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъva na desęte.

parole.significato: door, doors (portal of entry into a building or room)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *dvьrь, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dvigati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъvojь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъvojiti. By surface analysis, дво́є (dvóje) + -ї́ти (-jíty). Compare Russian двои́ть (dvoítʹ), Belarusian дваі́ць (dvaícʹ), Polish dwoić.

parole.significato: two (the digit/figure 2; a thing numbered thus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъvojьka. By surface analysis, дво́є (dvóje) + -ка (-ka). Compare Belarusian and Russian дво́йка (dvójka), Polish dwójka, Czech dvojka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъvojьnikъ. Compare Russian двойни́к (dvojník).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dvòrъ.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian дво́йчи (dvójči), from Old East Slavic дъвоичи (dŭvoiči), from Proto-Slavic *dъvojьťi. Cognate with Belarusian дво́йчы (dvójčy), Old Polish dwójcy. By surface analysis, дві (dvi) + -чі (-či).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъde.

parole.significato: about a person: hulking, large, broad-shouldered, strong, thick
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *debelъ.

From Middle Ukrainian девѧносто (devjanosto), from Old East Slavic девѧносъто (devęnosŭto), from Proto-Slavic *devę(t)nòsъto, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *newin(t)śimta, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥dḱomt. Compare Russian девяно́сто (devjanósto).

parole.significato: inula, elecampane (Inula spp., especially Inula helenium)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *devęsilъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *devętъ.
From Proto-Slavic *devętь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *devętь na desęte.
From Proto-Slavic *devętь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥.
From Old East Slavic дьнь (dĭnĭ), from Proto-Slavic *dьnь (“day”). Cognate with Belarusian дзень (dzjenʹ), Russian день (denʹ), Bulgarian ден (den), Sanskrit दिन (dina).

From Old East Slavic деревѧнꙑи (derevęnyi), from Proto-Slavic *dervěnъ, from Proto-Indo-European *derwēno- / *derwoyno-, from *deru- (see *dóru). Morphologically *dervo (“tree”) + *-ěnъ. Equivalent to де́рево (dérevo) + -я́ний (-jányj). Compare Russian деревя́нный (derevjánnyj), Belarusian драўля́ны
From Proto-Slavic *dervo, from Proto-Indo-European *dóru. Doublet of дре́во (drévo).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dernъ.

parole.significato: sod (the layer of earth in which grass grows)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *dьrnъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic дьржава (dĭržava), from Proto-Slavic *dьržava.

parole.significato: state (attributive) (of or relating to a nation state or its government)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian державный (deržavnyj), from Old East Slavic дьржавьныи (dĭržavĭnyi), from Proto-Slavic *dьržavьnъ. By surface analysis, держа́ва (deržáva, “state”) + -ний (-nyj, adjective-forming suffix). Compare Belarusian дзяржа́ўны (dzjaržáwny), Russian держа́вный (deržávnyj), Serbo-
Inherited from Old Ruthenian держа́ти (deržáti), from Old East Slavic держати (deržati), дьржати (dĭržati), from Proto-Slavic *dьržati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dьrzъkъ.

parole.significato: to tear, to tear apart, to tear up
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian де́рти (dérti), from Proto-Slavic *derti. Cognate with Slovene drẹ́ti, Czech dřít, Polish drzeć.
From Proto-Slavic *desętь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *déśimt. Cognates include Belarusian дзе́сяць (dzjésjacʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *desętъ.
From Proto-Slavic *desętь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *déśimt. Cognates include Belarusian дзе́сяць (dzjésjacʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dȅševъ.

parole.significato: spring (place where water emerges from the ground)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žerdlo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čьmeľь.

parole.significato: to ring, to jingle, to chime, to clink, to clank, to ding
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian дзвинѣти (dzviněti), from Old East Slavic звьнѣти (zvĭněti), from Proto-Slavic *zvьněti.

From Old Ruthenian дзвони́ти (dzvoníti), from Old East Slavic звонити (zvoniti), from Proto-Slavic *zvoniti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwen-. Cognates with Polish dzwonić, Serbo-Croatian зво̀нити.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zvonъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian зе́ркало (zérkalo), from Proto-Slavic *zьrkadlo, *zьrcadlo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *divakъ. By surface analysis, ди́во (dývo) + -а́к (-ák).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *divizna.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *divьnъ. By surface analysis, ди́во (dývo) + -ний (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dȋvo.
A compound derived from Proto-Slavic *dȋvo and *viděti, cognate with obsolete Polish dziwowidz and dziwowid.

parole.significato: to surprise, to amaze, to astonish, to astound
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *divovati. By surface analysis, ди́во (dývo) + -ува́ти (-uváty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dikъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dymъ.
From Old East Slavic дꙑнꙗ (dynja), from Proto-Slavic *dyňa.

parole.significato: child (a male or female child, a son or daughter)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dětę.
From Old East Slavic дѣтѧ (dětę), from Proto-Slavic *dětę.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dyxati.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian длꙗ (dlja), from Old East Slavic дьлꙗ (dĭlja), from Proto-Slavic *dьľa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dьnьsь, from *dьnь (“day”) + *sь (“this”). Reanalyzed as день (denʹ) + -сь (-sʹ).

parole.significato: bed (of a river), bottom (of a lake)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic дъно (dŭno), from Proto-Slavic *dъno (“bottom”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dubnas, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰubnos, from *dʰewb- (“deep”).

parole.significato: to, toward (it can indicate a general direction, instead of the final destination of the movement; see на)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian до (do), from Old East Slavic до (do), from Proto-Slavic *do, from Proto-Indo-European *de, *do.

parole.significato: to, up to, until (indicates reaching a certain (often implied) point in space or time)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian до- (do-), from Old East Slavic до- (do-), from Proto-Slavic *do.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian доба (doba, “time, period”), from Proto-Slavic *doba (“time”). Considering that sense 1 (day, nychthemeron) was absent in Old Ruthenian, it is likely a semantic loan from Polish doba.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dòbrъ dь̏nь.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian до́брый день (dóbryj denʹ), from Old East Slavic добрꙑи дьнь (dobryi dĭnĭ), from Proto-Slavic *dòbrъ dь̏nь. By surface analysis, univerbation of до́брий (dóbryj, “good”) + день (denʹ, “day”). Compare Polish dobrydzień, Belarusian дабры́дзень (dabrýdzjenʹ).

parole.significato: good, benign, genial, gentle, kind, kindly
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian до́брый (dóbryj), from Old East Slavic добръ (dobrŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dobrъ.

parole.significato: hello, good day, g'day, good afternoon
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dòbrъ dь̏nь. Literally, “good day”.

parole.significato: good (that which is correct or helpful)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic добръ (dobrŭ), in turn from Proto-Slavic *dòbrъ.
From Middle Ukrainian доброта (dobrota), from Old East Slavic доброта (dobrota), from Proto-Slavic *dobrota. Equivalent to до́брий (dóbryj) + -ота́ (-otá).

parole.significato: product, output, yield, gain (something that is obtained or acquired through work)
parole.testo: From добу́ти (dobúty, “to obtain, to acquire”) + -ок (-ok), from Old Ruthenian добитокъ (dobitok), добытокъ (dobytok), from Proto-Slavic *dobytъkъ. Compare Belarusian дабы́так (dabýtak), Bulgarian добитък (dobităk), Macedonian добиток (dobitok), Polish dobytek, Serbo-Croatian доби́так.

parole.significato: to hollow, to dig, to gauge, to slot, to hole
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dьlbati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dьlgъ.

From Old East Slavic дългота (dŭlgota), from Proto-Slavic *dьlgota. By surface analysis, до́вгий (dóvhyj) + -ота́ (-otá). Cognate with Belarusian даўгата́ (dawhatá), Russian долгота́ (dolgotá), Serbo-Croatian дуго̀та, Slovene dołgóta.

parole.significato: reprimand, reproof, rebuke, admonition, dressing-down, scolding
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ganīti, whence also га́нити (hányty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dodati. Cognate with Pannonian Rusyn додац (dodac) and Polish dodać.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dokazati. By surface analysis, до- (do-) + казати (kazaty)

parole.significato: how long, until when, until what time
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *do ka as if from до (do) + к (k) + -и (-y). Cognate with Serbo-Croatian до̏к, Macedonian докај (dokaj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dolati. Likely related to *odolěti, whence одолі́ти (odolíty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dolina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dolnь.
From Middle Ukrainian долото (doloto), from Old East Slavic долото (doloto), from Proto-Slavic *dolto, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dálbtan, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelbʰ-.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian до́лꙗ (dólja), from Old East Slavic долꙗ (dolja), from Proto-Slavic *doľa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dáljāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *delh₁- (“to divide”).

parole.significato: to pursue, to seek, to strive for (persevere in pursuit of)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *domagati, with -ся (-sja) suffix. Compare Russian домога́ться (domogátʹsja), Belarusian дамага́цца (damahácca), Polish domagać się, Slovak domáhať sa.

Inherited from Old East Slavic домови (domovi), домовь (domovĭ), from Proto-Slavic *domovi, the u-stem dative singular of *domъ (“home”). Cognate with Belarusian дамо́ў (damów). Doublet of до́мові (dómovi).
Deverbal from допитати (dopytaty). From Proto-Slavic *pytati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dorga.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dorgъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic досада (dosada), from Proto-Slavic *dosada.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *do syta. From до (do) + сит- (syt-, “satiated, full”) + -а (-a). Compare до́ста (dósta) and до́сить (dósytʹ).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian досыть (dosytʹ), from Proto-Slavic *do syti, from *sytь (“satiety”). Cognate with Polish dosyć, Old Church Slavonic до сыти (do syti).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *do sъta. Compare до́сита (dósyta) and до́сить (dósytʹ).
Inherited from Middle Ukrainian достатокъ (dostatok), from Old East Slavic достатъкъ (dostatŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dostatъkъ, from *dostati.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dostojьnъ. By surface analysis, до- (do-) + стоя́ти (stojáty) + -ний (-nyj). Compare Russian досто́йный (dostójnyj), Belarusian дасто́йны (dastójny), Polish dostojny, Bulgarian досто́ен (dostóen).

parole.significato: to achieve, to attain, to reach
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sęťi.
Abstract noun of дося́жни́й (dosjážnýj), from досягти́ (dosjahtý), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sęťi.

Inherited from Old East Slavic доходъ (doxodŭ), from Proto-Slavic *doxodъ. By surface analysis, deverbal from дохо́дити (doxódyty). Compare Russian дохо́д (doxód), Belarusian дахо́д (daxód), Polish dochód.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъždžь.

parole.significato: to milk (to express milk from mammal)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic доити (doiti), from Proto-Slavic *dojiti (“to give milk, milk”).

parole.significato: ladder (frame used for ascent and descent)
parole.testo: Possibly inherited from Proto-Slavic *drabina, from *drabь or *drabъ. Cognate with Polish drabina (see there for more) and Belarusian драбі́ны (drabíny).

parole.significato: to tease, to entice, to tempt
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drazniti. Doublet of дразни́ти (draznýty). Cognate with Belarusian дражні́ць (dražnícʹ), Russian дразни́ть (draznítʹ), Bulgarian дра́зня (dráznja), Polish drażnić.

parole.significato: to tease, to entice, to tempt
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drazniti. Doublet of дражни́ти (dražnýty). Cognate with Belarusian дражні́ць (dražnícʹ), Russian дразни́ть (draznítʹ), Bulgarian дра́зня (dráznja), Polish drażnić.

parole.significato: to annoy, to irritate, to irk, to get on the nerves of, to vex
parole.testo: Possibly from дра́ти (dráty) + -увати (-uvaty), from Proto-Slavic *dьràti. Cognate with Russian дратовать (dratovatʹ), Bulgarian дретат (dretat).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drevьnъ.. Doublet of да́вній (dávnij).

parole.significato: chills, trembling (from fear, cold, illness, etc.)
parole.testo: Derived from дрижати (dryžaty), from Proto-Slavic *drъžati (“to tremble, shiver”). By surface analysis, дрижати (dryžaty, “to tremble”) + -ак (-ak, “nominalizing suffix”) + -и (-y, “plural suffix”).

parole.significato: to quake, to quiver, to shake, to shiver, to tremble
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drъžati. Cognate with Russian дрожа́ть (drožátʹ), Polish drżeć.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dristati.

parole.significato: to crush, to comminute, to pulverize, to smash
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drobiti. Cognate with Russian дроби́ть (drobítʹ), Serbo-Croatian дро̀бити, Czech drobit, Polish drobić.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dъrva.

parole.significato: tremble, quiver, shiver, tremor, palpitation, shudder

From Proto-Slavic *družina (“team, company”), from *drugъ (“friend, companion”) + *-ina.

parole.significato: to be friends (with), to be on friendly terms (with)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *družiti. By surface analysis, друг (druh) + -и́ти (-ýty). Compare Russian дружи́ть (družítʹ), Belarusian дружы́ць (družýcʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *družьnъ. Parsable as друг (druh) + -ній (-nij).
From Proto-Slavic *drǫkъ, *drǫgъ.

parole.significato: to scratch, to claw, to scrape
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drapati. Soft "р" is probably of expressive origin, compare Slovak driapať for the same development. Doublet of дра́пати (drápaty) without soft "р". Cognate with Belarusian дра́паць (drápacʹ), Russian дра́пать (drápatʹ), Czech drápat, Polish drapać.
Inherited from Old East Slavic дрѧхлъ (dręxlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dręx(ъ)lъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drobь. Cognate with Russian дробь (drobʹ).

parole.significato: odds and ends, small things, small stuff
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian дробꙗзокъ (drobjazok), from Proto-Slavic *drobězgъ. The unexpected -і- in the root likely arose by analogy with дрібни́й, дріб (dribnýj, drib).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drobьnъ.
From Old East Slavic дрожди pl (droždi), from Proto-Slavic *droždžьje. Cognate with Belarusian дро́жджы (dróždžy) and Russian дро́жжи (dróžži).
From Proto-Slavic *drozdъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *trozdós, from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos.

parole.significato: to nap, to have a nap, to doze, to slumber, to drowse
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *drěmati, from Proto-Indo-European *drēm-ye-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”).

parole.significato: drowsiness, sleepiness, somnolescence, halfsleep, dogsleep, doze, snooze
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian дрѣмо́та (drěmóta), from Proto-Slavic *drěmota. By surface analysis, дріма́ти (drimáty) + -о́та (-óta).

parole.significato: oak (tree of the genus Quercus and its wood)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *dǫbъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰanw-.
From Old East Slavic дуга (duga), from Proto-Slavic *dǫga, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *dangāˀ.
From Proto-Slavic *dužь. Cognates include Russian дю́жий (djúžij), Belarusian ду́жы (dúžy), Polish duży.
From earlier гду́ля (hdúlja) and гду́ня (hdúnja), from Proto-Slavic *kъduňa, from Latin cydōnia, from Ancient Greek Κυδωνία (Kudōnía, “quince-tree”).
From Old East Slavic думати (dumati), from Proto-Slavic *dumati. Derived from Gothic 𐌳𐍉𐌼𐌾𐌰𐌽 (dōmjan) or Proto-Slavic *dъmǫ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *duplo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *durь.

parole.significato: to deceive, to fool, to dupe, to hoodwink, to bamboozle, to take in
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *duriti. By surface analysis, дур (dur) + -ити (-yty). Cognate with Russian дури́ть (durítʹ), Polish durzyć.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *durьnъ.
From Late Proto-Slavic *dǫti.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *duxmenъ.

parole.significato: confessor (a priest who hears confession and then gives absolution)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian духовникъ (duxovnik), from Proto-Slavic *duxovьnikъ (“cleric”). Compare Old Czech duchovník, Russian духовни́к (duxovník), Belarusian духо́ўнік (duxównik).
From Old East Slavic доуша (duša, “soul”), Proto-Slavic *duša.

parole.significato: mental, psychic (relating to the mind, psyche or soul)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dušěvьnъ. By surface analysis, душа (duša) + -ев(ий) (-ev(yj)) + -ний (-nyj). Compare Russian душе́вный (dušévnyj), Belarusian душэ́ўны (dušéwny).

parole.significato: to smother, to strangle, to choke, to suffocate
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dušiti (“to suffocate, to choke”). Cognate with Belarusian душы́ць (dušýcʹ), Russian души́ть (dušítʹ), Czech dusit, Polish dusić, Bulgarian душа́ (dušá), Slovene dušiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dȗšiti (“to sniff, to scent”). By surface analysis, дух(и) (dux(y)) + -ити (-yty). Cognate with Belarusian душы́ць (dušýcʹ), Russian души́ть (dušítʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dušьnъ. By surface analysis, дух (dux, “hot air”) + -ний (-nyj). Compare Polish duszny, Russian ду́шный (dúšnyj)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *degъtь.
From Proto-Slavic *dętelъ.

From Proto-Slavic *děvъka, a diminutive of *děva. By surface analysis, діва (diva) + -ка (-ka).
From дівка (divka) + -ина (-yna). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *děva (“maiden, girl”). Cognates include Belarusian дзяўчы́на (dzjawčýna), Polish dziewczyna.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dědъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děža.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dolъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děliti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dělo.

parole.significato: district, precinct (administrative subdivision, especially for electoral or policing purposes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dělьnica. Equivalent to діл(и́ти) (dil(ýty), “to divide”) + -ни́ця (-nýcja). Compare Polish dzielnica.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děľa.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian домъ (dom), from Old East Slavic домъ (domŭ), from Proto-Slavic *dȍmъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian дѣра (děra), from Old East Slavic дѣра (děra), from Proto-Slavic *děra.

parole.significato: to fetch, to take, to take out
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *dostavati. By surface analysis, ді- (di-, variant of до-) + става́ти (staváty). Compare Russian достава́ть (dostavátʹ), Belarusian дастава́ць (dastavácʹ), Polish dostawać.

parole.significato: to fetch, to take, to take out (from, e.g., the fridge or a box; followed by the preposition з. By contrast, брати is a…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dostati. Compare Russian доста́ть (dostátʹ), Belarusian даста́ць (dastácʹ), Polish dostać.

Derived from Old East Slavic дѣтъва (dětŭva) (compare derivation of мошкара (moškara)), from Proto-Slavic *dětъva. Compare Polish dziatwa. By surface analysis, Old East Slavic дѣтъва (dětŭva) + -ор (-or) + -а (-a).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *děti.
From Proto-Slavic *děti.

Inherited from Old East Slavic дѣꙗти (dějati), from Proto-Slavic *dějati, an extension of Proto-Slavic *děti (“to do, to say”).

parole.significato: stresses the topic; is, really, right, isn't it, etc. (used as a tag question would be in English)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic же (že), from Proto-Slavic *že, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ge, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰi. Cognate with Czech že, Ancient Greek γε (ge), Sanskrit हि (hi), Russian же (že).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žaba.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žaga.

parole.significato: to covet, to crave, to thirst for, to hunger for, to ache
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian жадати, жедати (žadati, žedati), from Old East Slavic жадати (žadati), from Proto-Slavic *žędati. Sense 3 is probably a semantic loan from Polish żądać.
From Old East Slavic жадьнъ (žadĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žędьnъ (“avid, greedy”).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian жалити (žaliti), from Proto-Slavic *žędliti. By surface analysis, жа́ло (žálo) + -ити (-yty).

parole.significato: sting (pointed portion of an insect or arachnid used for attack)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žędlo.

Inherited from Old East Slavic жалоба (žaloba, “mourning, grief”), from Proto-Slavic *žaloba. The second meaning (complaint) probably developed under the influence of Russian жа́лоба (žáloba, “complaint”).

parole.significato: regret, grief, sorrow (emotional pain on account of something done or experienced in the past, with a wish that it had…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žalь.

parole.significato: pity (a feeling of sympathy at the misfortune or suffering of someone or something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žalostь. Compare Russian жа́лость (žálostʹ), Polish żałość.

parole.significato: to feel sorry for, to pity, to feel pity for
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *želěti (“to regret”).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian жаръ (žar), from Old East Slavic жаръ (žarŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žārъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰēr- (“heat”, root noun), from *gʷʰer- (“heat, hot”), whence also Proto-Slavic *gorěti, whence Ukrainian горі́ти (horíty, “to burn”).

parole.significato: to roast, to fry, to broil, to grill
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian жа́рити (žáryty), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *žàriti. Cognates include Russian жа́рить (žáritʹ), Belarusian жа́рыць (žárycʹ).

parole.significato: hot, sultry, torrid (weather, climate, air, sun)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žarъkъ.

parole.significato: harvest (process of harvesting, gathering the ripened crop, harvest yield)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic жѧтва (žętva), from Proto-Slavic *žętva, from *žęti + *-tva. By surface analysis, жати (žaty) + -тва (-tva).
From Proto-Slavic *žęti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gémtei; cognate with Old Church Slavonic жѧти (žęti), 1sg. жьмѫ (žĭmǫ).
From Proto-Slavic *žęti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *genˀtei; cognate with Old Church Slavonic жѧти (žęti), 1sg. жьнѭ (žĭnjǫ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žasъ.

parole.significato: to burn (to cause something to be consumed by fire; to cause burns or a burning sensation in something)

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ženixъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian жердь (žerdʹ), from Old East Slavic жьрдь (žĭrdĭ), from Proto-Slavic *žьrdь.
