Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žerbę, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrebʰ-. Cognate with Belarusian жарабя́ (žarabjá), Old Church Slavonic жрѣбѧ (žrěbę), Polish źrebię.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žerbьcь, from *žerbę, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrebʰ-. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic жрѣбѧ (žrěbę), Bulgarian жребе́ц (žrebéc), Polish źrebiec (“colt”). Compare Ancient Greek βρέφος (bréphos, “baby, foetus”).

parole.significato: lot (anything (as a die, pebble, ball, or slip of paper) used in determining a question by chance, or without human cho…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žerbъkъ, a diminutive of Proto-Slavic *žerbъ. By surface analysis, жереб (žereb) + -ок (-ok).

parole.significato: to devour, to gobble, to gorge oneself on, to scoff (eat greedily)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic жерети (žereti), from Proto-Slavic *žèrti.

parole.significato: to live, to dwell, to stay (to have reside somewhere permanently or temporarily)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian жива́ти (živáti), from Proto-Slavic *živati.
From Proto-Slavic *živъ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).

parole.significato: to nourish, to feed, to nutrify, to sustain
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *živiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *životъ.

In Western Ukraine, євре́й (jevréj) is historically more pejorative than жид (see Khrushchev quote in the Russian entry)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žila.

parole.testo: From Old East Slavic жиръ (žirŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žirъ. The sense "clubs" is from a now-obsolete sense of "acorn". Acorns are one of the four suits in German-suited decks and were adapted by French card makers as the clubs suit. Compare Serbo-Croatian жир (“acorn; acorns (the card suit)”), Polish

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian жити (žyty), from Proto-Slavic *žìti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gīˀwetei, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti. Cognate to Lithuanian gyventi, Sanskrit जीवति (jīvati), Latin vīvō.
Inherited from Middle Ukrainian жито (žyto), from Proto-Slavic *žito (“grain, corn”).

parole.significato: the palm with the fingers bent so that they could scoop up, grab or hold something
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian жме́нꙗ (žménja, “handful”), from Proto-Slavic *žьmьnь, *žьmьňa, with -я (-ja).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьlknǫti. By surface analysis, жовч (žovč) + -нути (-nuty). Compare Belarusian жо́ўкнуць (žówknucʹ).
From Old Ruthenian жолтый (žoltyj), from Old East Slavic жьлтъ (žĭltŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žьltъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *gilˀtás, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zьlčь.

parole.significato: trough (a long, narrow container, open on top, for feeding or watering animals)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian жолобъ (žolob), from Old East Slavic жолобъ (žolobŭ), желобъ (želobŭ), from Proto-Slavic *želbъ.

parole.significato: to chow down, to eat up, to devour, to gorge on
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *želpati.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian жолудь (žoludʹ), from Old East Slavic желѫдь (želǫdĭ), from Proto-Slavic *žȅlǫdь.
From Old Ruthenian жона (žona), rom Old East Slavic жена (žena), from Proto-Slavic *žena, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *génāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn.

The epenthetic 'r' might have arisen under the influence of шорстки́й (šorstkýj, “rough, rigid”), compare dialectal жестки́й (žestkýj). Cognate with Belarusian жо́рсткі (žórstki) and

Inherited from Old Ruthenian жесто́кий (žestókij), from Old East Slavic жестокъ (žestokŭ), from Proto-Slavic *žestokъ. The epenthetic 'r' might have arisen by analogy with жорстки́й (žorstkýj). Cognate with Russian жесто́кий (žestókij).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьrьcь, from *žьrti + *-ьcь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *girˀ-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerH-.

parole.significato: to chew, to masticate, to munch
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žьvati (“to chew”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žukъ.
From Old East Slavic жеравль (žeravlĭ), from Proto-Slavic *žeravľь. Cognates include Belarusian жураве́ль (žuravjélʹ) and Russian жура́вль (žurávlʹ).

parole.significato: to afflict, to grieve, to sadden (cause sorrow or distress to)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *žuriti.

parole.significato: from (from inside a place, e.g., a building or a geographical place)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *jьz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰs.

parole.significato: with (somebody, with a comitative meaning; otherwise, to express "with/using/through something" with an instrumental me…
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *sъ(n), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom.

parole.significato: attached to imperfective verbs to form the perfective aspect
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic з-, с- (z-, s-), from Old East Slavic з-, съ- (z-, sŭ-), from Proto-Slavic *sъ(n)-. Doublet of со- (so-) from Old Church Slavonic съ- (sŭ-), as well as doublet of ко-, ком-, кон-, сим- and син- (ko-, kom-, kon-, sym- and syn-).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian з-, уз-, вз- (z-, uz-, vz-), from Old East Slavic въз-, въс- (vŭz-, vŭs-), from Proto-Slavic *vъz-. Doublet of воз- (voz-) from Old Church Slavonic въз- (vŭz-).

parole.significato: attached to imperfective verbs to form the perfective aspect
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian з-, с-, из- (z-, s-, iz-), from Old East Slavic из-, ис- (iz-, is-), from Proto-Slavic *jьz-. Doublet of екс- (eks-).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *za.

From Middle Ukrainian забавный (zabavnyj), from Old East Slavic забавьныи (zabavĭnyi), from Proto-Slavic *zabavьnъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian за́баван, Belarusian заба́ўны (zabáwny), Polish zabawny.

parole.significato: to beat in, to drive in, to hammer in, to bang in, to ram in (to insert with blows: nail, post, stake, wedge, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zabiti. By surface analysis, за- (za-, prefix) + би́ти (býty, imperfective verb). Compare Russian заби́ть (zabítʹ), Belarusian забі́ць (zabícʹ), Polish zabić.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zabobonъ. Compare Belarusian забабо́ны (zababóny), Polish zabobon.
Derived from Proto-Slavic *borniti. Cognates include Belarusian забаро́на (zabaróna)

parole.significato: to forbid, to prohibit, to ban
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian заборони́ти (zaboroníti), from Proto-Slavic *zaborniti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + борони́ти (boronýty). Cognates include Old Church Slavonic забранити (zabraniti), Serbo-Croatian забра́нити, Belarusian забарані́ць (zabaranícʹ) and Polish zabronić.
From Proto-Slavic *zaby̋ti, the same root as забу́ти (zabúty). Compare Russian забыва́ть (zabyvátʹ), Belarusian забыва́ць (zabyvácʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zabỳti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + бу́ти (búty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zavada. By surface analysis, deverbal from зава́дити (zavádyty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian заутра (zautra), заутро (zautro), завтра (zavtra), завтро (zavtro), from Old East Slavic заоутра (zautra), from Proto-Slavic *za utra. Cognate with Belarusian за́ўтра (záwtra), Serbo-Croatian су̏тра, Slovak zajtra, Slovene zájtra (“tomorrow morning”).
From Proto-Slavic. Cognate with Russian завиру́ха (zavirúxa), Belarusian завіру́ха (zavirúxa), Polish zawierucha.
Related to віра (vira). From Proto-Slavic *věra.

parole.significato: to perish, to die (lose one's life, especially in a sudden violent way)
parole.testo: From за- (za-) + гиба́ти (hybáty) (dialectal), from Old East Slavic гꙑбати (gybati), from Proto-Slavic *gybati. Compare Bulgarian заги́вам (zagívam).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gordъ.

parole.significato: danger (exposure to or instance of liable harm)
parole.testo: From за- (za-) + гроза́ (hrozá, “terror”), from Proto-Slavic *groza (“terror”).

parole.significato: to lose, to mislay, to misplace (cause to cease to be in one's possession or capability due to unfortunate or unknown c…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zagubiti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + губи́ти (hubýty). Compare Russian загуби́ть (zagubítʹ), Belarusian загубі́ць (zahubícʹ), Polish zagubić.

parole.significato: unit, detachment, squad, force, brigade, unit
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *gъnati.

parole.significato: back, back part, back side, rear
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zadъ.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian заздрити, зазрѣти (zazdriti, zazrěti), from Old East Slavic зазьрѣти (zazĭrěti, “to judge, to envy, to be tempted”), from Proto-Slavic *zazьrěti. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic зазьрѣти (zazĭrěti), Polish zazdrościć. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + здрі́ти (zdríty).

parole.significato: to encroach, to infringe, to trespass (on, upon: на + accusative)
parole.testo: From за- (za-) + зіха́ти (zixáty, “to yawn”) (obsolete) (whence also позіха́ти (pozixáty)), from Proto-Slavic *zěxati, related to *zěvati (“to yawn”) (whence зіва́ти (ziváty) / зівну́ти (zivnúty)). Compare Slovene zazẹ́hati.

parole.significato: superfluous, redundant (beyond that which is needed)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zàjьvъ.

parole.significato: occupation, occupying, taking possession of, act of aggression
parole.testo: Ultimately за- (za-) + Proto-Slavic *jьmati (“to have, possess”) + -ання (-annja), or from Proto-Slavic *ęti (“to take”).

parole.significato: to bewitch, to enchant, to cast a spell on, to charm, to ensorcel
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian заклина́ти (zaklináti), from Old East Slavic заклинати (zaklinati), from Proto-Slavic *zaklinati. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + -клина́ти (-klynáty).
From Middle Ukrainian законъ (zakon), from Proto-Slavic *zakonъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zakopati. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + копа́ти (kopáty). Compare Russian закопа́ть (zakopátʹ), Belarusian зака́паць (zakápacʹ), Polish zakopać.
From Proto-Slavic *želza. Cognate with Russian железа́ (železá).
From Middle Ukrainian желѣзо (želizo), зелѣзо (zelizo), from Old East Slavic желѣзо (želězo), from Proto-Slavic *želězo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zamerti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + ме́рти (mérty). Compare Belarusian заме́рці (zamjérci), Polish zamrzeć, Russian замере́ть (zamerétʹ).
From Proto-Slavic *zamogti. Cognate with Belarusian замо́жны (zamóžny), Polish zamożny.
From Proto-Slavic *zamъkъ, deverbal from *zamъknǫti.

Inherited from Old East Slavic за мужь (za mužĭ, literally “behind the husband”), from Proto-Slavic *za + *mǫ̑žь. Compare Russian за́муж (zámuž), Old Church Slavonic за мѫжь (za mǫžĭ), Polish za mąż, Slovene zamož.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zapęstьje. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + п'ясть (pʺjastʹ) + -я (-ja). Cognate with Russian запя́стье (zapjástʹje).

parole.significato: to light, to light up, to ignite (cause to burn: cigarette, flame, furnace, match, stove, torch etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zapaliti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + пали́ти (palýty). Compare Russian запали́ть (zapalítʹ), Belarusian запалі́ць (zapalícʹ), Polish zapalić.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zapeťi. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + пекти́ (pektý). Compare Russian запе́чь (zapéčʹ), Belarusian запячы́ (zapjačý), Polish zapiec.
From за- (za-) + плю́щити (pljúščyty). Possibly derived from Proto-Slavic *ploskъ (literally “'flat'”).
From Proto-Slavic *zapovědь, later reanalyzed by analogy with Proto-Slavic *zavětъ. Cognate with Belarusian запаве́т (zapavjét); compare also the normative Russian заве́т (zavét).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zapustiti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + пусти́ти (pustýty). Compare Russian запусти́ть (zapustítʹ), Belarusian запусці́ць (zapuscícʹ), Polish zapuścić, Serbo-Croatian запу̀стити/zapùstiti.
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *radi.
From Proto-Slavic *zaraza. Analyzable as a deverbal from зарази́ти (zarazýty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zaraziti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + рази́ти (razýty). Compare Russian зарази́ть (zarazítʹ), Belarusian заразі́ць (zarazícʹ), Polish zarazić.

parole.significato: merit (something deserving or worthy of positive recognition or reward)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zasluga.

parole.significato: to deserve, to merit, to be worthy of, to earn (followed by direct object, genitive case or на (na) + accusative)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zaslužiti. Compare Russian заслужи́ть (zaslužítʹ), Belarusian заслужы́ць (zaslužýcʹ), Polish zasłużyć, Czech zasloužit.

parole.significato: closure (a device to facilitate temporary and repeatable opening and closing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zatvorъ, related to *zavorъ (“closure, enclosure”), from *verti. The introduction of -t- results from rebracketing of the prefix *otъ- of *otъvorìti.

parole.significato: calm, lull (period of reduced wind, waves, noise or activity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zatišьje. By surface analysis, за́тишок (zátyšok) + -я (-ja). Compare Russian зати́шье (zatíšʹje), Belarusian заці́шша (zacíšša), Polish zacisze.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zatorъ. Compare Polish zator.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zaxodъ. Cognate with Polish zachód (“west, sunset”), Serbo-Croatian zahod (“sunset”).

parole.significato: to conceive, to beget, to engender
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian зачати (začati, “to begin, to conceive”), from Old East Slavic зачѧти (začęti), from Proto-Slavic *začęti. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + -ча́ти (-čáty)

parole.significato: to conceive, to beget, to engender
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian зачина́ти (začináti, “to begin, to conceive”), from Old East Slavic зачинати (začinati), from Proto-Slavic *začinati. By surface analysis, за- (za-) + -чина́ти (-čynáty).

parole.significato: to state, to declare, to announce
parole.testo: From за- (za-) + яви́ти (javýty), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *aviti. Compare Russian заяви́ть (zajavítʹ).
From Proto-Slavic *zajęcь, *zajьcь (“hare, hopper, jumper”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъbožьje. By surface analysis, з- (z-) + бог (boh) + -я (-ja).
From Proto-Slavic *sъborъ. Doublet of собо́р (sobór, “cathedral”), a borrowing from Old Church Slavonic.
From збір (zbir) + -ник (-nyk), from Proto-Slavic *sъborъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian зва́ти (zváti), from Old East Slavic зъвати (zŭvati), from Proto-Slavic *zъvati, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewH-.

parole.significato: to get used, to become accustomed (to: до (+ genitive) / infinitive)
parole.testo: з- (z-) + -ви́кнути (-výknuty), from Old East Slavic вꙑкнути (vyknuti), from Proto-Slavic *vyknǫti. Compare Polish zwyknąć.

parole.significato: to twine, to weave, to plait, to twist
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian зви́ти (zvíti), from Old East Slavic съвити, *възвити (sŭviti, *vŭzviti) and извити (izviti), from Proto-Slavic *sъviti, *vъzviti and *jьzviti. By surface analysis, з- (z-) + вити (vyty).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian звы́чай (zvýčaj), from Old East Slavic съвычаи (sŭvyčai), from Proto-Slavic *sъvyčajь. Compare Polish zwyczaj.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zvǫkъ.

Genitive singular form of Old East Slavic отъколѣ (otŭkolě) from Proto-Slavic *otkoljь. The presence of і rather than o in the penultimate syllable is likely due to the influence of the earlier form відкі́ль (vidkílʹ). Prefixed with з- (z-).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *gvězda.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zvěrь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьzvorъ.

parole.significato: animal, animal's (of or relating to animals)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian звѣри́ный (zvěrínyj), from Proto-Slavic *zvěrinъ. By surface analysis, звір (zvir) + -и́ний (-ýnyj).
Derived from зві́дати (zvídaty), perfective of ві́дати (vídaty), from Proto-Slavic *věděti. Literally зві́сно means "known".
Inherited from Old Ruthenian зга́га (zháha), from Proto-Slavic *jьzgaga.
From Proto-Slavic *jьzgoda. Cognate with Polish zgoda.

parole.significato: to burn down (to burn completely, so that nothing remains)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian згорѣти (zhority) and изгорѣти (yzhority), from Old East Slavic изгорѣти (izgorěti), from Proto-Slavic *jьzgorěti. By surface analysis, з- (z-) + горі́ти (horíty). Compare Russian сгоре́ть (sgorétʹ), Belarusian згарэ́ць (zharécʹ), Polish zgorzeć.
From Proto-Slavic *sъdorvьje. Morphologically, from здоро́вий (zdoróvyj) + -'я (-ʺja).
From Old East Slavic здоровъ (zdorovŭ), from Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ.
Variant of зрі́ти (zríty). From Old East Slavic зьрѣти (zĭrěti, “to see, to ripen”), from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁-.
Inherited from Middle Ukrainian [Term?], from Old East Slavic зеленꙑи (zelenyi), from Proto-Slavic *zelènъjь.
From Proto-Slavic *zemľa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źémijāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰéǵʰōm.

parole.significato: earth (attributive) (of or relating to earth as in soil or ground)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian земляный (zemljanyj), *землѧныи (*zemljanyj), from Old East Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *zemľanъ. By surface analysis, земля́ (zemljá) + -яни́й (-janýj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zemьnъ.
From Proto-Slavic *zьrno, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm.
From Proto-Slavic *zima, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źeimā́ˀ.
From Proto-Slavic *zimьnъ. Morphologically, from зима́ (zymá) + -ний (-nyj). Related to зи́мній (zýmnij).

parole.significato: winter, wintry (of or pertaining to winter)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *zimьnъ. Morphologically, from зима́ (zymá) + -ній (-nij). Related to зи́мний (zýmnyj).

parole.significato: to glance, to cast glances, to glimpse, to peek (to periodically look at)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zьrkati, probably remodeled after -зира́ти (-zyráty). Cognate with Polish zerkać.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъlъ.
From зли́тися (zlýtysja) + -я (-ja). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *liti (“to pour”), whence лити (lyty).
Inherited from Old East Slavic зъло (zŭlo), from Proto-Slavic *zъlo.

parole.significato: malice, maliciousness, spite, anger, rancour (UK), rancor (US) (strong feeling of displeasure, hostility or antagonism…
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic зълоба (zŭloba), from Proto-Slavic *zъloba, from *zъlъ + *-oba. By surface analysis, злий (zlyj) + -оба (-oba).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъlodějь. Cognates include Belarusian зло́дзей (zlódzjej), Polish złodziej with the same meanings. The Russian злоде́й (zlodéj) means "villain".
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъločinъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъločinьcь. Compare Belarusian злачы́нец (zlačýnjec) and Czech zločinec.

parole.significato: morel (any of several fungi in the genus Morchella)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *smъrčьkъ. By surface analysis, змо́рщ(ити) (zmóršč(yty), “to wrinkle”) + -ок (-ok).
From Proto-Slavic *zmьjь. Related to змія́ (zmijá).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьzměna.
From Proto-Slavic *zmьja. Related to змій (zmij).
From з- (z-) + Proto-Slavic *najьti (“to find”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *znakъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *znamenitъ, from *znàmę. Compare Russian знамени́тый (znamenítyj), Polish znamienity.
From Proto-Slavic *znamę, generalized into a second-declension noun.

From Middle Ukrainian знати (znaty), from Old East Slavic знати (znati), from Proto-Slavic *znati, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-. Cognate with Carpathian Rusyn зна́ти (znáty), Russian знать (znatʹ), Belarusian знаць (znacʹ), etc.

Inherited from Old East Slavic знати (znati), from Proto-Slavic *znati, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źnōˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵnéh₃t (“to know, get to know”), from *ǵneh₃-. The relation of this word to зна́ти (znáty, “to know”) was from mediaeval Slavic nobility being noteworthy for their high
From Proto-Slavic *značiti. Equivalent to знак (znak) + -ити (-yty). Cognate with Russian зна́чить (znáčitʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *znobiti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *jьzъ nova. Compare Belarusian зноў (znow). By surface analysis, з- (z-) + нов (nov)
Inherited from Old East Slavic [Term?], from Proto-Slavic *jьzъ nova. Compare Polish znowa, Russian снова (snova). Equivalent to з- (z-) + нову (novu).

parole.significato: to remove, to take away, to take off, to take down
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *sъnęti, from *sъ(n)- + *ęti. Reanalyzed as з- (z-) + -(й)ня́ти (-(j)njáty). Compare Russian снять (snjatʹ), Belarusian зняць (znjacʹ).
From Proto-Slavic *sъ(n), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom.
Inherited from Old East Slavic зьдъчии (zĭdŭčii, “potter, builder, bricklayer, mason”), from зьдъ (zĭdŭ, “stone wall”), зьдати (zĭdati), from Proto-Slavic *zьdati (“to build”).
Inherited from Old East Slavic золото (zoloto), from Proto-Slavic *zolto, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰolh₃tom (o-grade), from *ǵʰelh₃- (“green, yellow”).
From Proto-Slavic *zořa. With -я (-ja).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъrǫčьnъ. Probably from з руки́ (z ruký) + -ний (-nyj).
From Proto-Slavic *zьrělъ. Cognates include Russian зре́лый (zrélyj), Bulgarian зрял (zrjal).
From Old East Slavic зьрѣти (zĭrěti, “to ripen”), from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵerh₂-.
From Middle Ukrainian зьрѣти (zʹrity), from Old East Slavic зьрѣти (zĭrěti, “to see”), from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti (“to look”). Further connections beyond Balto-Slavic unclear.

From Middle Ukrainian зубъ (zub), from Old East Slavic зѫбъ (zǫbŭ), from Proto-Slavic *zǫbъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *źámbas, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos. Cognate to Old Church Slavonic зѫбъ (zǫbŭ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zǫbatъ. By surface analysis, зуб (zub) + -а́тий (-átyj). Compare Belarusian зуба́ты (zubáty), Polish zębaty, Czech zubatý, Lower Sorbian zubaty.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zǫbrъ.
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sъrěsti.
From Proto-Slavic *sъrěsti. Cognates include Belarusian сустрэча (sustreča) and Serbo-Croatian сусрет. Related to Russian встреча (vstreča) and Polish pośrześć.
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sъrěsti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zęba.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian зѧбнꙋти, зꙗбнꙋти (zjabnuti, zjabnuti), from Old East Slavic зѧбнꙋти (zębnuti), from Proto-Slavic *zębnǫti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zętь, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁-.

parole.significato: to gape, to be wide open
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian зья́ти (zʹjáti), from Old East Slavic зьꙗти (zĭjati), from Proto-Slavic *zьjati.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian зѣва́ти (zěváti), from Old East Slavic зѣвати (zěvati), from Proto-Slavic *zěvati.

parole.significato: potion (a small portion or dose of a liquid which is medicinal, poisonous, or magical)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zelьje (“vegetation, herbs”). With -я (-ja).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zěnica.

parole.significato: to yell, to shout, to scream, to cry, to bawl
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zěpati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zorъ. Akin to зріти (zrity, “(archaic) to see, to look”).
зоря́ (zorjá) + -ка (-ka), from Proto-Slavic *zořa. Cognates include Belarusian зо́рка (zórka). The term звізда́ (zvizdá) was discontinued in Ukrainian.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *zorъkъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьkati.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ęti (“to take”), reanalyzed after the verbs prefixed with *vъn-, *sъn- (vъn-ęti → vъ-nęti, sъn-ęti → sъ-nęti). The "й" at the front arose by analogy with йма́ти (jmáty), іма́ти (imáty).

parole.significato: an idiot, a simpleton, a stupid person.
parole.testo: Compare with Belarusian е́луп (jélup), Belarusian ёлупень (jólupjenʹ); Polish jołop; dialectal Russian ело́п (jelóp). Some linguists connect this word to Proto-Slavic *jalovъ (“idle, barren (for animals)”), while others suggest it was derived from Tatar (compare with Tatar юләр (yülär, “stupid, a fo
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъ(n).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koblǫkъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кадити (kaditi), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kadìti.
From Old East Slavic казати (kazati), from Proto-Slavic *kazati. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeǵ-.

parole.significato: to damage, to spoil, to disfigure, to uglify
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian кази́ти (kazíti), from Old East Slavic казити (kaziti), from Proto-Slavic *kaziti.

parole.significato: to rage, to get furious, to get mad
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian кази́тисѧ (kazítisja, “to spoil, to get damaged, to suffer”), from Old East Slavic казитисѧ (kazitisę, “to spoil, to get damaged, to change for the worse”), from Proto-Slavic *kaziti sę. By surface analysis, кази́ти (kazýty) + -ся (-sja).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kakati. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kakka-. Compare Serbo-Croatian kakati, kakiti, Italian cacare.
Inherited from Old East Slavic калъ (kalŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kalъ (“dirt”).

parole.significato: to knock, to bang, to pound
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian калата́ти, колата́ти (kalatáti, kolatáti), from Old Ruthenian колоти́ти (kolotíti), from Proto-Slavic *koltiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kalina.
From Proto-Slavic *kaľuža or *kaluža, related to *kalъ (“dirt”). Cognate with Polish kałuża.
From Old East Slavic камень (kamenĭ), accusative of камꙑ (kamy), from Proto-Slavic *kamy.

parole.significato: to drip, to drop, to trickle, to dribble
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ка́пати (kápati), from Old East Slavic капати (kapati), from Proto-Slavic *kapati.

By metathesis from Old East Slavic пакость (pakostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *pakostь (“vicissitude”), whence also па́кість (pákistʹ). Likely formed in the northern dialects, as it has the suffix -ость (-ostʹ) rather than the expected -ість (-istʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kara (“punishment”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *karasь.
From Old East Slavic карати (karati), from Proto-Slavic *karati.

parole.significato: to take for a ride/drive, to drive sb. around (for no particular reason or for fun)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian *ката́ти (*katáti), from Old East Slavic ката́ти (katáti), from Proto-Slavic *katati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kočanъ.

parole.significato: to wring (using a mangle), to mangle (laundry)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian кача́ти (kačáti), from Old East Slavic *кача́ти (*kačáti), from Proto-Slavic *kaťati.
From Old East Slavic каша (kaša), from Proto-Slavic *kaša.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kaš(ь)ľь (“cough”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kaʔs(u)lio-, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂s-.
From Proto-Slavic *kašьľati (“to cough”), from *kašьľь (“cough”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kāˀsulia, *kāˀslia, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂s-.

parole.significato: to repent, to regret (to feel sorrow or regret for what one has done or omitted to do)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic каꙗтисѧ (kajatisę), from Proto-Slavic *kàjati, with reflexive -ся (-sja) suffix. Compare Russian ка́яться (kájatʹsja), Belarusian ка́яцца (kájacca).

parole.significato: to hurry, to hasten, to rush, to press, to precipitate
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ква́пити (kvápiti), from Proto-Slavic *kvapiti. Cognate with Belarusian ква́піць (kvápicʹ), Czech kvapit, Polish kwapić.

parole.significato: kvass (a type of fermented no- or low-alcohol beverage, made from bread, often flavored with fruit)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian квасъ (kvas), from Old East Slavic квасъ (kvasŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kvasъ (“leaven, fermented drink”). Cognate with Latin cāseus whence English cheese, and Sanskrit क्वथ् (kvath, “to boil”).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ква́сити (kvásiti), from Old East Slavic *квасити (*kvasiti), from Proto-Slavic *kvasiti. Causative of ки́снути (kýsnuty).

From Proto-Slavic *květьnь from Proto-Slavic *květъ. Related to квітка (kvitka, “flower”), referring to flowers which bloom at this time of year, with -ень (-enʹ). Cognates include Polish kwiecień (“April”), Czech květen (“May”), Russian цве́тень (cvétenʹ, “April (archaic)”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrma, remodeled after керува́ти (keruváty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyvati.

parole.significato: to throw, to cast, to fling
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic кидати (kidati), from Proto-Slavic *kydati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyjь.

parole.significato: to throw, to cast, to fling, to hurl
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kydnǫti.

Derived from the same root as кипі́ти (kypíty, “to boil”), from Proto-Slavic *kypě̀ti, from Proto-Indo-European *kwep-, whence English covet and hope. Compare Russian кипяти́ть (kipjatítʹ), Belarusian кіпяці́ць (kipjacícʹ).

parole.significato: to boil, to simmer, to seethe
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *kypě̀ti, from Proto-Indo-European *kwep-, whence English cupidity, covet and hope.
From Proto-Slavic *kys(ь)lъ as киснути (kysnuty) + -лий (-lyj)
Inherited from Old Ruthenian *киснꙋти (*kisnuti) (attested in закиснꙋти, скиснꙋти (zakisnuti, skisnuti)), from Old East Slavic кꙑснꙋти (kysnuti), from Proto-Slavic *kysnǫti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kystь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyselь. Compare Belarusian кісель (kisjelʹ), Polish kisiel, and Russian кисель (kiselʹ). By surface analysis, кислий (kyslyj) + -іль (-ilʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyšьka.

parole.significato: to swarm, to teem (to move as a swarm; to be rife)
parole.testo: Possibly inherited from Proto-Slavic *kyšěti. Compare Russian кише́ть (kišétʹ), Belarusian кішэ́ць (kišécʹ). Related to Lithuanian kušė́ti (“to move”) and to Latvian kustēt and kušņāt (“to move”).

parole.significato: to bow, to bow down (to bend oneself as a gesture of respect or deference) (to somebody: + dative case)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klaňati, iterative of *kloniti, whence клони́ти (klonýty), with stress shift from second to first syllable (stress on either syllable was present in Ukrainian in the 19th century). Compare Russian кла́няться (klánjatʹsja), Belarusian кла́няцца (klánjacca).

parole.significato: scrap, shred, snippet (a fragment; a detached, incomplete portion)
parole.testo: Possibly inherited from Proto-Slavic *klapъtь.

parole.significato: to put, to place, to lay
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klasti, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂-.
From Proto-Slavic *kъlějь or *kъlьjь or *klějь or *klьjь. Cognate with Polish klej.

parole.significato: maple, maple tree (Acer gen. et spp.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klenъ.

parole.significato: to peen, to hammer (the blade of a scythe (or a different instrument) in order to sharpen and straighten it)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian клепа́ти (klepáti), from Old East Slavic клепати (klepati), from Proto-Slavic *klepati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klikati.

parole.significato: to bend, to incline, to lean, to tilt
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kloniti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klopotъ.
From Proto-Slavic *kľučь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *kljaukjas, from Proto-Indo-European *klewk-yo-s, from *kle(h₂)uk-, an extended form of *(s)kleh₂w- (“hook, key, peg”).

parole.significato: to curse, to execrate, to damn (imprecate evil upon)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klęti. Compare Russian клясть (kljastʹ), Belarusian клясці́ (kljascí), Polish kląć.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian клѧтва (kljatva), from Old East Slavic клѧтва (klętva), from Proto-Slavic *klętva. By surface analysis, кля́сти (kljásty) + -тва (-tva).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klěpati, the iterative of Proto-Slavic *klepati, *klepnǫti.

parole.significato: cage, coop (an enclosure made of bars, normally to hold animals)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic клѣтъка (klětŭka), from Proto-Slavic *klětъka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klěščь.

parole.significato: tongs (an instrument or tool used for picking things up without touching them with the hands or fingers, consisting of…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *klěšča. Doublet of кліщ (klišč)
From Proto-Slavic *kъňiga.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъnorzъ. Cognate with Polish knur.

parole.significato: the wife or consort of a ruling monarch: queen, duchess
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъnęgyni.; compare Russian княги́ня (knjagínja), Serbo-Croatian кнѐгиња, Slovene knegínja (tonal orthography). By surface analysis, княг- (knjah-) + -и́ня (-ýnja). князь (knjazʹ) is derived from Early Proto-Slavic *kuningu, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz, with з by the ap

parole.significato: a young prince, a child of a prince
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian кнѧжѧ́ (knjažjá), княжа́ (knjažá), from Proto-Slavic *kъnęžę. Equivalent to князь (knjazʹ) + -я (-ja).

parole.significato: the monarch of a state or a principality: prince, king, duke
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian князь m (knjazʹ, “a prince”), кнѧ́зь m (knjázʹ), from Old East Slavic [Term?], from Proto-Slavic *kъ̏nędzь m (“a prince”). Doublet of ксьондз (ksʹondz) and кінг (kinh).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kobyla.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kovàľь. By surface analysis, кований (kovanyj) + -аль (-alʹ).
From Proto-Slavic *kovàti (“to hew, to forge”) + -ний (-nyj).

From Middle and Old Ukrainian колбаса́ (kolbasá), Old East Slavic кълбаса (kŭlbasa). Slavic cognates point to several reconstructed forms (Proto-Slavic *kъlbasa, *klobasa, *kobasa), indicating that this is a very early borrowing, with no clear antecedent. Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъlzati.

Inherited from Old East Slavic кользъкъ (kolĭzŭkŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kъlzъkъ. By surface analysis, ковз- (kovz-) + -кий (-kyj). Cognates include Czech kluzký, Polish kiełzki, Belarusian ко́ўзкі (kówzki), (dialectal) Russian ко́льзкий (kólʹzkij), Russian ско́льзкий (skólʹzkij).
From Proto-Slavic *kъltati, which is parallel to *glъtati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъltunъ. Cognate with Belarusian каўту́н (kawtún), Russian колту́н (koltún), and Polish kołtun.
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kokotъ, possibly via Old Slovak kohút. Compare Carpathian Rusyn and Pannonian Rusyn когут (kohut).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kogъtь.
From Proto-Slavic *kody, cognate with Polish kiedy, Slovak kedy, Russian када (kada).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koža.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ко́жен (kóžen), from Proto-Slavic *kožьde with -ен (-en).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ко́жный (kóžnyj), from Proto-Slavic *kožьde with -ний (-nyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kožuxъ. By surface analysis, ко́жа (kóža, “skin”) + -ух (-ux).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koza.
From Old East Slavic козьлъ (kozĭlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kozьlъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kozyrь (“shield made of goat skin”), from *koza (“goat”). Modern sense likely originates from the fact that a trump beats other cards (i.e. covers them).

parole.significato: basket, handbasket (chiefly made of bast or wicker)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kozubъ (“bag, pouch, basket made of bark”), from *koza (“goat”). Compare Polish kozub.
From Old East Slavic колєсѣ (kolesě), the dual number of коло (kolo), from Proto-Slavic *kolo, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷekʷlom (“circle”), *kʷékʷlos (“circle”).
From Proto-Slavic *kolě, cognate with Belarusian калі́ (kalí), Bulgarian коле (kole), Russian коли (koli) and Slovene koli.

parole.significato: to rock, to sway, to swing (move gently from side to side or backward and forward)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolyxati. Compare Russian колыха́ть (kolyxátʹ), Belarusian калыха́ць (kalyxácʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kȍlo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolovortъ. Sense 3 is a calque of Russian коловра́т (kolovrát).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolovortъ.
From Old East Slavic колода (koloda), from Proto-Slavic *kolda.

parole.significato: well (hole sunk in the ground and used as a source of water)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic колодязь (kolodjazĭ), from Proto-Slavic *koldędzь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolodějь.

parole.significato: ear, spike (fruiting body of a grain plant)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kȏlsъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolti.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian колоти́ти (kolotíti), from Proto-Slavic *koltiti.

parole.significato: to poke, to dig [with direct object or в (v) or у (u, + locative), along with instrumental ‘with something’] (to prod o…
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps a result of contamination of Proto-Slavic *kopati (whence копа́ти (kopáty, “to dig”)) and *lupati (whence лупа́ти (lupáty, “to pound, to chip/split off”)), or by addition of ko- to *lupati. Compare Russian колупа́ть (kolupátʹ), Belarusian калупа́ць (kalupácʹ).

parole.significato: koliada, a Christmas folk tradition, common in Ukraine, featuring people going around singing Christmas carols and rece…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolęda, from Latin kalendae. Doublet of кале́нди (kaléndy).

parole.significato: Koledari, caroling in the Eastern European style
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic [Term?], Proto-Slavic [Term?]. Cognate to Bulgarian коледуване (koleduvane), Macedonian коледарење (koledarenje), Russian колядова́ние (koljadovánije), Belarusian калядава́нне (kaljadavánnje). Equivalent to колядува́ти (koljaduváty, “to carol”) + -ання (-annja, “nominalizer”).
From Old East Slavic колѣно (kolěno), from Proto-Slavic *kolěno.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolěja. Related to *kolo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *komarъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *komaxa. Morphologically, most likely from the onomatopoeic root Proto-Indo-European *komH- (“to hum”) + -аха (-axa).

parole.significato: pantry, larder, storeroom, cellar (room in a house used to store produce)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *komora, from Latin camera or Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “arch, vault”).

parole.significato: a thick tree-branch attached to the trunk; a bough
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *konarъ. Cognate with Polish konar.

parole.significato: to be in one's death throes, to be in one's death agonies, to die, to expire
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *konati. Compare Belarusian кана́ць (kanácʹ), Polish konać.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian коне́чный (konéčnyj), from Old East Slavic коньчьнꙑи (konĭčĭnyi), from Proto-Slavic *konьčьnъ.

parole.significato: hemp, cannabis (plant of the genus Cannabis)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *konopľa (“hemp”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *konьčina.

parole.significato: groom, stableman, hostler (person at an inn who looks after horses)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic конюхъ (konjuxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *koňuxъ. By surface analysis, кінь (kinʹ) + -ух (-ux).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koňušьna. By surface analysis, ко́нюх (kónjux) + -ня (-nja).

parole.significato: sixty pieces of something (e.g. sheaves of hay or rye, eggs, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopa. Compare Belarusian капа́ (kapá), Russian копа́ (kopá).
From Proto-Slavic *kopanь, morphologically from копа́ти (kopáty, “to dig, to ditch”) + -нь (-nʹ).
From Old East Slavic копати (kopati), from Proto-Slavic *kopati.
From Proto-Slavic *kopyto, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós.
Probably inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopnǫti. By surface analysis, копа́ти (kopáty) + -ну́ти (-núty). Compare Russian копну́ть (kopnútʹ), Belarusian капну́ць (kapnúcʹ).
From Old East Slavic кора (kora, “bark”), from Proto-Slavic *kora (“bark”), from Proto-Indo-European *ker-.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian корабль (korablʹ), from Old East Slavic корабль (korablĭ), from Proto-Slavic *korabľь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koristьnъ. Cognate with Polish korzystny.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koristь. Compare Russian коры́сть (korýstʹ), Belarusian кары́сць (karýscʹ), Polish korzyść.

parole.significato: to scold, to reprimand, to criticize
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koriti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koryto.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кърмъ (kŭrmŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kъrmъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrmiti.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian коро́бка (koróbka), from Old East Slavic коробъка (korobŭka), from Proto-Slavic *korbъka. By surface analysis, ко́роб (kórob) + -ка (-ka).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *korva.

parole.significato: korovai (large, single-piece round or rectangular loaf of bread, elaborately decorated and served at a wedding)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic короваи (korovai), from Proto-Slavic *korvajь. Cognate with Russian карава́й (karaváj), Bulgarian крава́й (kraváj), Serbo-Croatian кра̀ва̄ј (“type of cake fed to the bride and groom”) (genitive крава́ја), Slovene kravȃj, krávaj. Per Vasmer, probably related to коро́ва
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xorǫgy.
From Old East Slavic король (korolĭ), from Proto-Slavic *korľь. Doublet of кріль (krilʹ).

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *korsta.

parole.significato: to spend, to pass, to while away, to kill (time)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian корота́ти (korotáti), from Proto-Slavic *kortati. By surface analysis, коро́т(кий) (korót(kyj)) + -ати (-aty).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian коротити (korotiti), from Old East Slavic *коротити (*korotiti), from Proto-Slavic *kortiti. By surface analysis, коро́т(кий) (korót(kyj)) + -ити (-yty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ.

parole.significato: to desire strongly, to yearn, to itch, to be impatient (to do something: +infinitive)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrtiti.
From Proto-Slavic *kr̥čь ~ *kъrčь; cf. Polish karcz, Kashubian kårč, Czech krč, and Slovene kŕč.
From Proto-Slavic *kъrčь; cf. Polish kurcz, Czech křeč, and Slovene krč.

parole.significato: to contort, to twist, to tense
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ко́рчити (kórčiti), from Old East Slavic *кърчити (*kŭrčiti), from Proto-Slavic *kъrčiti.

parole.significato: tavern, inn where spirits are sold (in Ukraine or Belarus before the Russian Revolution)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *kъrčьma.
From Proto-Slavic *kъrčьmařь, possibly via a West Slavic or South Slavic language. Compare Russian корчма́рь (korčmárʹ), Belarusian карчма́р (karčmár), Polish karczmarz.

parole.significato: to uproot, to root up, to eradicate, to extirpate, to grub up
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrčevati. By surface analysis, корч (korč) + -ува́ти (-uváty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian коренне, коренье (korenne, korenʹje), from Proto-Slavic *korenьje. Cognate with Old Church Slavonic кореньѥ (korenĭje), Czech koření, Slovak korenie. From корінь (korinʹ) + -і́ння (-ínnja)
From Proto-Slavic *kory, with -інь (-inʹ, Etymology 2). Cognate with Russian ко́рень (kórenʹ).
From Proto-Slavic *kosa.

parole.significato: tilted, sloping, slanted, oblique, askew, inclined (not erect or perpendicular; not parallel to, or at right angles fro…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian косый (kosyj), from Old East Slavic косъ (kosŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kosъ.

parole.significato: to scythe, to reap, to mow
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kositi. Cognate with Russian коси́ть (kosítʹ), Belarusian касі́ць (kasícʹ), Old Church Slavonic косити (kositi), Polish kosić.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kotьlъ, borrowed from Gothic 𐌺𐌰𐍄𐌹𐌻𐍃 (katils), from Proto-Germanic *katilaz, possibly borrowed from Latin catīllus (“small bowl”), from catīnus (“food-vessel”) + -lus (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: to roll (to impel forward by causing to turn over and over on a supporting surface)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian коти́ти (kotíti), from Old East Slavic *коти́ти (*kotíti), from Proto-Slavic *kotiti.

parole.significato: to have young, to bear offspring
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kotìti sę. Compare Russian коти́ться (kotítʹsja), Belarusian каці́цца (kacícca), Polish kocić się.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kotorъjь, *koterъjь, definite of **kotorъ
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kotorъjь, *koterъjь, definite of **kotorъ, **koterъ.

parole.significato: To love, to have a strong romantic or sexual affection for someone.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koxati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *košara.

From Proto-Slavic *košuľa, from Vulgar Latin casula (“cloak”).

parole.significato: to commit, to do (usually something bad)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kojiti (“to soothe”), the exact nature of the semantic shift is unknown. Compare Old Ruthenian ко́итися (kóitisja, “to be held, to be soothed”). Alternatively, related to чини́ти (čynýty).
From Proto-Slavic *kravьcь (compare *krojiti (“to cut”)).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian крадѣ́жъ, краде́жъ (kradě́ž, kradéž), from Proto-Slavic *kradežь. By surface analysis, крад- (krad-) + -іж (-iž).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian кра́плѧ (kráplja), from Old East Slavic краплꙗ (kraplja), from Proto-Slavic *krapľa. By surface analysis, кра́пати (krápaty) + -я (-ja).
Inherited from Old East Slavic краса (krasa), from Proto-Slavic *krasa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krasьnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krasti.

parole.significato: to cut up, to slice, to carve up
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian краꙗти (krajati), from Old East Slavic краꙗти (krajati), from Proto-Slavic *krajati (compare *krojiti). Cognate with Belarusian кра́яць (krájacʹ), Polish krajać.
From Old East Slavic краина (kraina), from Proto-Slavic *krajina. Cognate with Russian краи́на (kraína), Belarusian краі́на (kraína), Polish kraina, Serbo-Croatian кра̏јина / krȁjina, etc.

parole.significato: to jag, to shred, to hack
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *krem- + *-sati, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krem-, from *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Compare Russian кромса́ть (kromsátʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kremy, with -інь (-inʹ, Etymology 2). Compare Russian кремень (kremenʹ), Belarusian крэмень (kremjenʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kresadlo. By surface analysis, креса́ти (kresáty) + -ло (-lo). Cognate with Czech křesadlo, Slovak kresadlo.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian креса́ти (kresáti), from Proto-Slavic *kresati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krečetъ.
From Proto-Slavic *krъvavъ, from *kry, with -авий (-avyj). Compare Belarusian крыва́вы (kryvávy), Polish krwawy, Russian крова́вый (krovávyj).

parole.significato: wrong, injustice (an instance of wronging someone; violating someone's rights)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian кривда (kryvda), from Old East Slavic кривьда (krivĭda), from Proto-Slavic *krivьda.

parole.significato: to wrong, to mistreat, to abuse, to hurt
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krivьditi, from Proto-Slavic *krivьda. Equivalent to кри́вда (krývda) + -ити (-yty). Compare Czech křivdit, Polish krzywdzić.
From Proto-Slavic *krivъ + -ий (-yj)

parole.significato: scream, cry, shriek outcry, shout, shouting, yell
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krikъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kridlo.

parole.significato: well, spring (a structure used as a source of water from the ground)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krinica.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kryti.
From earlier *кр̥ха́ (*kr̥xá), inherited from Proto-Slavic *krъxa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krěxъkъ. By surface analysis, кри́ха́ (krýxá) + -ки́й (-kýj).
кри́хта (krýxta, “crumb”) + -ний (-nyj). Ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *krъxa. Compare Russian кро́хотный (króxotnyj).

parole.significato: to shout, to cry, to holler, to yell
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kričati.

parole.significato: to crumble, to crumb, to break into pieces
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krъšiti. Cognate with Russian кроши́ть (krošítʹ), Serbo-Croatian кр̀шити.
From кри́ха́ (krýxá) + -ка (-ka), from Proto-Slavic *krъxa.
From Proto-Slavic *kry, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *krū́ˀs, from Proto-Indo-European *kréwh₂s (“blood of a wound”).
From Proto-Slavic *kopriva or *kropiva.

parole.significato: to sprinkle, to splash, to spritz, to spatter (to cover with drops of something)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian кропити (kropiti), from Old East Slavic кропити (kropiti), from Proto-Slavic *kropiti.

parole.significato: to cut, to cut out (fabric, leather, etc. to make clothes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian кроити (kroiti), from Old East Slavic кроити (kroiti), from Proto-Slavic *krojiti. With -їти (-jity).

parole.significato: disc (UK), disk (US) (region of a plane bounded by a circle)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫgъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫglъ. By surface analysis, круг (kruh) + -лий (-lyj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krukъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫtъ.

parole.significato: to spin, to turn, to rotate
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krǫtiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krušiti.
From Proto-Slavic *krozě. Cognate with Bulgarian кръз (krăz), Serbo-Croatian кро̏з, Czech krůz, Slovak kroz.

parole.significato: except, except for, apart from, aside from, with the exception of
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *kromě, locative case of *kroma (“edge, boundary”). Cognate with Slovak okrem, Belarusian акрамя́ (akramjá), Czech kromě, Pannonian Rusyn окрем (okrem), and Russian кро́ме (króme)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kropъ.

parole.significato: to fasten, to fix in place, to secure in place
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian крѣпити (kripyty), from Proto-Slavic *krěpiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krěpъkъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian крѣпость (krěpostʹ), from Old East Slavic крѣпость (krěpostĭ), from Proto-Slavic *krěpostь (“strength”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krěslo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *krъtъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъtyrь.

parole.significato: large still, tank, vat (for distillation or boiling of liquids)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kubъ (“wooden vessel/dish”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kovàti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫda.

parole.significato: smithy, smithery, forge (a place where a smith works; a workshop in which metals are shaped by heating and hammering th…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kuzňa.
From Proto-Slavic *kǫkoľь, *kǫkolъ.

parole.significato: to limp, to hobble (to walk lamely)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kulьgati. Compare Belarusian кульга́ць (kulʹhácʹ), Russian кульга́ть (kulʹgátʹ), Czech kulhat, Polish (obsolete) kulhać (synonym of kuleć), Slovak kuľhať.
From Proto-Slavic *kumъ, back-formation from *kuma (“godmother”) (whence also кума́ (kumá)), from Balkan Vulgar Latin *cómmater, from Latin compater (“godfather”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kunica.
From Old East Slavic купа (kupa), from Proto-Slavic *kupa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫpati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kupьcь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kupiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kupľati. By surface analysis, куп- (kup-) + -яти (-jaty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian купова́ти (kupováti), from Old East Slavic куповати (kupovati), from Proto-Slavic *kupovati. By surface analysis, куп- (kup-) + -увати (-uvaty). Cognate with Czech kupovat, Polish kupować, Bulgarian купу́вам (kupúvam) and Serbo-Croatian купо̀вати.

parole.significato: font, baptismal font (a large basin with holy water used for baptism)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian кꙋпѣль (kupělʹ), from Old East Slavic кꙋпѣль (kupělĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kǫpělь. In the Christian context, a semantic loan from Old Church Slavonic кѫпѣль (kǫpělĭ, “font”). By surface analysis, купа́ти (kupáty) + -іль (-ilʹ).
Compare dialectal кур (kur, “rooster, cock”), ку́ра (kúra, “hen”), куря́ (kurjá, “chick”) (t-stem); from Old East Slavic куръ (kurŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kurъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic кꙋрити (kuriti, “smoke, emit smoke”), from Proto-Slavic *kuriti.
From Proto-Slavic *kura + ка (ka).

From Proto-Slavic *kuropъtъka, a diminutive of Proto-Slavic *kuropъty. The modern form arose through consonant cluster simplification (*куропътъка › *курі́птка › курі́пка). Cognate with Belarusian курапа́тка (kurapátka). Russian куропа́тка (kuropátka).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫsati.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian кꙋсокъ (kusok), from Proto-Slavic *kǫsъkъ. By surface analysis, кус (kus) + -ок (-ok).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫtъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫtati. Cognate with Russian ку́тать (kútatʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kucъ.
From Old East Slavic кѫча (kǫča), from Proto-Slavic *kǫťa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kučeravъ. By surface analysis, ку́чер (kúčer, “curl”) + -я́вий (-jávyj). Compare Russian кучеря́вый (kučerjávyj), Belarusian кучара́вы (kučarávy), Slovak kučeravý.

Related to Old East Slavic кꙋчма (kučma), Russian ку́чма (kúčma), Belarusian ку́чма (kúčma), Polish kuczma, Czech kučma, Slovak kučma, Serbo-Croatian ку̑чма / kȗčma, Slovene kúčma, Bulgarian ку́чма (kúčma), кушма́ (kušmá), and probably inherited from Proto-Slavic *kučьma, which is related to Proto-S

Inherited from Old Ruthenian кꙋшати (kušati, “to taste, to eat”), from Old East Slavic кꙋшати (kušati), from Proto-Slavic *kušati, the sense "to eat" is most likely a semantic loan from Russian ку́шать (kúšatʹ, “to eat”) and was not inherited from Old Ruthenian.

parole.significato: to taste, to try (to sample the flavor of something orally)
parole.testo: From ку́шати (kúšaty) + -увати (-uvaty), from Proto-Slavic *kušati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kusťь, from *kustъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kobьcь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kogъtь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolъ.
From Old East Slavic колико (koliko), from Proto-Slavic *koliko. Doublet of скі́льки (skílʹky).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kolьce. By surface analysis, ко́ло (kólo) + -це (-ce, diminutive suffix).
From Old East Slavic коньць (konĭcĭ, “end; edge, border”), from Proto-Slavic *konьcь (“end”). Compare Russian коне́ц (konéc), Belarusian кане́ц (kanjéc), Polish koniec.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian кончи́ти (končíti), from Proto-Slavic *konьčiti. By surface analysis, кіне́ць (kinécʹ) + -ити (-yty).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian кунь (kunʹ), конь (konʹ), from Old East Slavic конь (konĭ), from Proto-Slavic *kòňь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopъtь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kostъka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kostь.

parole.significato: male cat, tomcat (domestic feline; member of Felidae family)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic котъ (kotŭ), from Proto-Slavic *kotъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *koty.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian ко́тка (kótka), from Old East Slavic ко́тъка (kótŭka), from Proto-Slavic *kòtъka. Equivalent to кіт (kit) + -ка (-ka). Cognate with Bulgarian ко́тка (kótka), Polish kotka.
From Old East Slavic кошь (košĭ), from Proto-Slavic *košь. Cognate to Polish kosz, Serbo-Croatian кош, etc.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ко́шка (kóška), from Old East Slavic *ко́чька (*kóčĭka), from Proto-Slavic *kòťьka. Cognate with Belarusian ко́шка (kóška), Russian ко́шка (kóška).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lava.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lagoda.

parole.significato: to fix, to mend, to repair
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lagoditi, from *lagoda. Compare Polish łagodzić.
From Proto-Slavic *ladъ, of unknown origin.

parole.significato: to get along, to be on good terms
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian *ла́дити (*láditi), from Old East Slavic ладити (laditi), from Proto-Slavic *laditi. By surface analysis, лад (lad) + -ити (-yty).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ла́до (ládo), from Old East Slavic ла́да (láda), from Proto-Slavic *lada.

parole.significato: to climb (up, on to), to scramble
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *laziti.
By surface analysis, ла́яти (lájaty, “to bark, to scold”) + -ка (-ka). Ultimately from Old East Slavic лаꙗти (lajati, “to bark, to scold”), from Proto-Slavic *làjati (“to bark”).
From Proto-Slavic *lajьno. Compare Belarusian лайно́ (lajnó), Bulgarian лайно́ (lajnó), Macedonian лајно (lajno), Polish łajno. Parsable as лій (lij) + -но (-no).

parole.significato: to break, to smash, to fracture
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lamati. Compare Russian лома́ть (lomátʹ), Polish łamać.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lomъkъ. By surface analysis, лам(а́ти) (lam(áty)) + -ки́й (-kýj).
From Proto-Slavic *lapa, according to Vasmer, cognate with Proto-Germanic *lōfô (“the palm or hollow of the hand”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lasъ.
From Proto-Slavic *lasica ~ *laska.
From Proto-Slavic *làska (“caress”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *laskavъ. Parsable as ла́ска (láska) + -а́вий (-ávyj). Compare Russian ла́сковый (láskovyj), Belarusian ла́ска́вы (láskávy), Polish łaskawy.

parole.significato: rags, rags and tatters, duds (very old, torn clothes; tattered clothes)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *loxmotьje with, by surface analysis, -я (-ja) suffix. Compare Russian лохмо́тья (loxmótʹja), Belarusian лахмо́цце (laxmóccje).

parole.significato: to scold, to berate, to chide, to dress down, to upbraid, to rail (at/against), to rip into
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic лаꙗти (lajati, “to bark, to scold”), from Proto-Slavic *làjati (“to bark”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *le, *lě.
From Proto-Slavic *olbǫdь, from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós (“white”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lьvъ.
From Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ, with -ий (-yj).
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *le da čь, *le da čьto (“anything”); *le da čьjь (“anyone's”). Compare Polish ladaco (“good-for-nothing”), lada (“any; paltry”).

parole.significato: to lie (to be in a horizontal position; usually followed by the preposition на and the locative case)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ležati (“to be lying [down]”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lemešь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lepetъ. Parallel to Old Church Slavonic лопотивъ (lopotivŭ, “stuttering”) (with o-grade).

parole.significato: to flatter, to adulate, to stroke someone's ego (to compliment someone, often insincerely and sometimes to win their fa…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian ле́стити (léstyty), from Old East Slavic льстити (lĭstiti), from Proto-Slavic *lьstiti. By surface analysis, (archaic or rare) лесть (lestʹ) + -ити (-yty).
From Middle Ukrainian лесть (lestʹ, “deception; seduction”) + -ощі (-ošči), from Old East Slavic льсть (lĭstĭ), from Proto-Slavic *lьstь.
From Old East Slavic летѣти (letěti), from Proto-Slavic *letěti. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lēk- (“to hop”).

parole.significato: vice (UK), vise (US) (mechanical screw apparatus used for clamping)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *leščetь, *leščedь, related to *leskati (“to strike”). Compare Polish leszczota (“splint”) (related, per Brückner, to Polish kleszcze (“forceps, pincers; pliers”)), Belarusian ляшчо́ткі (ljaščótki), кляшчо́тка (kljaščótka).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lъža, from *lъgati + *-ja; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- and *-yeh₂. Compare Bulgarian лъжа́ (lăžá).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *li .

parole.significato: ski (one of a pair of long flat runners designed for gliding over snow)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lyža, if existing in Proto-Slavic at all. Cognate with Russian лы́жа (lýža).

parole.significato: ski (one of a pair of long flat runners designed for gliding over snow)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lyži, if existing in Proto-Slavic at all.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lizati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *liznǫti. By surface analysis, лиза́ти (lyzáty) + -ну́ти (-núty). Compare Russian лизну́ть (liznútʹ), Belarusian лізну́ць (liznúcʹ), Polish liznąć.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *linǫti. By surface analysis, ли́ти (lýty) + -нути (-nuty). Semantically influenced by леті́ти (letíty) and пли́нути (plýnuty).
From Proto-Slavic *lipa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *léiˀpāˀ.

From Proto-Slavic *lipa. Related to ли́па (lýpa, “linden”), referring to linden trees which bloom at this time of year, with -ень (-enʹ). Cognates include Belarusian ліпень (lipjenʹ, “July”), Polish lipiec, Russian липец (lipec), and Serbo-Croatian lipanj (“June”).
From ли́па (lýpa, “linden”) + -ець (-ecʹ), from Proto-Slavic *lipa.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lipъkъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lьpnǫti, synonym of *lьpěti. Compare Russian ли́пнуть (lípnutʹ), Belarusian лі́пнуць (lípnucʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lisъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lysъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lisьjь. By surface analysis, лиси́ця (lysýcja) + -ий (-yj)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *listъ (“leaf”).

parole.significato: November (eleventh month of the Gregorian calendar)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic листопадъ (listopadŭ, “October”), from Proto-Slavic *listopadъ (“leaf fall; time of leaf fall”), from *listъ (“leaf”) + *pasti (“to fall”). Cognates include Czech listopad (“november”) and Serbo-Croatian listopad (“october”).
From Proto-Slavic *listьje. Morphologically equivalent to лист (lyst) + -я (-ja). Compare Russian ли́стья (lístʹja), Bulgarian ли́сте (líste).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *liti (“to pour”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lixva.

parole.significato: evil, wicked, naughty; capable of causing harm or evil
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lixъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lixodějь. By surface analysis, ли́хо (lýxo, “evil”) + ді́яти (díjaty, “to do”). Cognates include Russian лиходе́й (lixodéj), Belarusian ліхадзе́й (lixadzjéj).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lice.

parole.significato: to suit, to look good on
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian личити (ličiti), from Proto-Slavic *ličiti. By surface analysis, лик (lyk) + -ити (-yty). Doublet of лічи́ти (ličýty).
Inherited from Old East Slavic лише (liše), originally comparative form of лихъ (lixŭ, “bad”), from Proto-Slavic *liše, лихо (lyxo) + -е (-e). Compare with Russian лишь (lišʹ).

parole.significato: to leave, to abandon, to part from, to forsake (to depart from; to separate from)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic лишити (lišiti), from Proto-Slavic *lišiti. By surface analysis, лих (lyx) + -и́ти (-ýty). Cognate with Russian лиши́ть (lišítʹ), Serbo-Croatian ли́шити, Czech lišit.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian лобъ (lob), from Old East Slavic лобъ (lobŭ), лъбъ (lŭbŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lъbъ.
From Proto-Slavic *loboda or *olboda.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lovъ.

parole.significato: to catch (to seize or intercept an object moving through the air or some other medium)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *loviti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lože.

parole.significato: to lay, to put, to place
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic ложити (ložiti), from Proto-Slavic *ložiti. Causative of лежа́ти (ležáty). Cognate with Russian ложить (ložitʹ), Belarusian лажыць (lažycʹ), Czech ložit, and Polish łożyć.

parole.significato: spoon (scooped utensil for eating or serving)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic лъжька (lŭžĭka), from Proto-Slavic *lyžьka, from *lъga (“bending”) + *-ъka.
From Proto-Slavic *lomъ.

parole.significato: to break, to break up, to break off, to snap, to snap off
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ломи́ти (lomíti), from Old East Slavic ломити (lomiti), from Proto-Slavic *lomiti.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian лоно (lono), from Old East Slavic лоно (lono), from Proto-Slavic *lono.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lopata.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lopuxъ.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *laskotati, from *laskati. Compare Belarusian ласката́ць (laskatácʹ), Polish łaskotać. The cause of the vowel shift is unclear but possibly influenced by Polish łoskotać (“to bang, to make a din”) and/or cognates thereof.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lososь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lǫgъ.
From Middle Ukrainian лукъ (luk), from Old East Slavic лукъ (lukŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lǫkъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lankás, from Proto-Indo-European *lenk- (“to bend”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lǫka.

Inherited from Old East Slavic лукавъ (lukavŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lǫkavъ. Cognate with Russian лука́вый (lukávyj), Bulgarian лука́в (lukáv), Serbo-Croatian лу̏кав, Old Church Slavonic лѫкавъ (lǫkavŭ).
Inherited from Old East Slavic лукавьство (lukavĭstvo), from Proto-Slavic *lǫkavьstvo. By surface analysis, лука́вити (lukávyty) + -ство (-stvo).

parole.significato: harrier (bird of prey in the genus Circus of the subfamily Circinae)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *luňь. Cognate with Russian лунь (lunʹ, “harrier”), Church Slavonic лунь (lunĭ, “vulture”), Serbo-Croatian type of kite (bird), Slovene lȗnj (“kite (bird)”), Czech luňak (“kite (bird)”). Per Vasmer, possibly from earlier *lupňь from Proto-Slavic *lupiti (“to peel”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lupiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lupiti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *laupī́ˀtei.

parole.significato: scales (small, flat and hard pieces of keratin covering the skin of an animal, particularly a fish or reptile)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *luska.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lučìti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lǫčiti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lánkīˀtei.

parole.significato: rather, would better (do something) (often used with verbs in the past tense with subjunctive би (by))
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lučьjь.

parole.significato: peel, rind (outer layer of a fruit, vegetable, etc.)
parole.testo: Related to (dialectal) лушпа́ (lušpá), variant of (obsolete) лу́спа́ (lúspá), inherited from Proto-Slavic *luspa.

parole.significato: to shell, to shale, to unhusk, to hull, to pod
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *luščiti. By surface analysis, луска́ (luská) + -ити (-yty).
Inherited from Old East Slavic льнъ (lĭnŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lьnъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *lína, from Proto-Indo-European *linom. Doublet of ли́на (lýna).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ľubъ + -ий (-yj).

parole.significato: to like, to love (platonically or aesthetically)
parole.testo: From Middle Ukrainian любити (ljubyty), from Old East Slavic любити (ljubiti), from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ljaubī́ˀtei, from Proto-Indo-European *lowbʰéyeti, from *lewbʰ-.

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian любо́въ f (ljubóv, nominative and accusative), from Proto-Slavic *ľubъ̀vь f (accusative of nominative *ľubỳ f). Cognate with Belarusian любо́ў f (ljubów); Russian любо́вь f (ljubóvʹ); etc.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ľudъ.

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian лю́ди pl (ljúdy, nominative), from Proto-Slavic *ľȗdi m pl (accusative of nominatives *ľȗdьjē m pl and *ľȗďē m pl). Cognate with Belarusian лю́дзі m pers pl (ljúdzi); Russian лю́ди m anim pl (ljúdi); etc.

parole.significato: man, person, human being, singular of люди (ljudy) (a people, folk, mankind, men)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *ľudina, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ- (“men, people”).

parole.significato: human (of or belonging to the species Homo sapiens)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ľudьskъ. By surface analysis, люд (ljud, “people, folk”) + -ський (-sʹkyj). Compare Polish ludzki, Belarusian людскі́ (ljudskí), Russian людско́й (ljudskój).

parole.significato: February (second month of the Gregorian calendar)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *ľutъ + -ий (-yj). Cognates include Belarusian лю́ты (ljúty) and Polish luty (“February”).

parole.significato: to enrage, to infuriate, to madden
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ľutiti. By surface analysis, лют- (ljut-) + -и́ти (-ýty).
Possibly a deadjectival of лю́тий (ljútyj), from Proto-Slavic *ľutъ.

parole.significato: to lie down (to assume a horizontal position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian лꙗгати (ljahati), from the earlier Old Ruthenian лѣгати (lěhati) with the root лѣг- (lěh-) leveled with the nasalized forms: Old Ruthenian лѣчи → лѧже, лѧгѫ, лꙗжъ (lěči → ljaže, ljahu, ljaž), from Old East Slavic лѣгати (lěgati), from Proto-Slavic *lěgati (see *leťi). parole.significato: a clearing in a forest (especially one prepared for sowing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lędo (“uncultivated land, clearing”). Cognate with Russian ля́до (ljádo), Polish ląd, and English land. Doublet of ля́до (ljádo).

parole.significato: a pine tree growing in a clearing
parole.testo: From ля́да (ljáda) + -ина (-yna). Compare Russian ляди́на (ljadína), Belarusian лядзі́на (ljadzína). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *lędina.

parole.significato: an elevated place in a forest overgrown with timber pines
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lędo (“uncultivated land, clearing”). Cognate with Russian ля́до (ljádo), Polish ląd, and English land.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lęděninъ, the ethnic name underlying лях (ljax, “Pole”).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian лѧхъ (ljax), from Old East Slavic лѧхъ (lęxŭ), from Proto-Slavic *lęxъ, from *lęděninъ.

parole.significato: bream, carp bream, common bream (fish of the species Abramis brama, considered the only member of the genus Abramis)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *leščь, from *leskati, *leščati, ultimately onomatopoeic. Compare Russian лещ (lešč), Belarusian лешч (lješč), Polish leszcz.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lěvъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ledъ.

parole.significato: to climb (up, on to), to scramble

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lȍjь.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lěnь.

parole.significato: to model, to mould, to shape (form into a particular shape)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic лѣпити (lěpiti), from Proto-Slavic *lěpiti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lěsъ (“tree, forest”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *letъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *lětati, frequentative from *letěti.

parole.significato: summer (attributive), estival (of or pertaining to summer)

From Proto-Slavic *lěto (“summer”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁tom.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *męta.

parole.significato: to rumple, to crumple, to wrinkle, to fumble, to crease

parole.significato: to lure, to alure, to entice

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mastidlo. By surface analysis, масти́ти (mastýty) + -ло (-lo).

parole.significato: to grease, to oil, to lubricate

parole.significato: stepmother (wife of one's biological parent, other than one's biological mother)

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian медъ (med), from Old East Slavic медъ (medŭ), from Proto-Slavic *mȅdъ.

parole.significato: lungwort, pulmonaria (plant of the genus Pulmonaria)

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *meďa.

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mьrzěti (“to loathe, to abhor”).

parole.significato: abhorrent, abominable, disgusting, loathsome, nasty, odious, repulsive, vile (inducing sensory or moral disgust)
parole.testo: From obsolete мерзи́ти (merzýty), from Proto-Slavic *mьrzěti.

parole.significato: to disgust, to revolt, to repulse, to repel

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mьrznǫti.

parole.significato: to dim, to fade, to go out
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ме́ркнути (mérknuti), from Old East Slavic мьркнꙋти (mĭrknuti), from Proto-Slavic *mьrknǫti.
From Proto-Slavic *mьrtvъ, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, *mr̥tós, ultimately from the root *mr̥-, *mer- (“to die”).

parole.significato: to live, to reside (to have permanent residence)

parole.significato: to flicker, to glimmer, to shimmer, to twinkle (to burn or shine unsteadily, or with a wavering light)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian мигати (mihati), from Old East Slavic мигати (migati), from Proto-Slavic *migati.

From dialectal Proto-Slavic *mězgyrь. Related to Russian мизги́рь (mizgírʹ).

parole.significato: to spare, to show mercy, to have mercy, to mercy

Inherited from Proto-Slavic *mimo.

parole.significato: to pass, to pass by, to go by, to go past
