Inherited from Old East Slavic чехолъ (čexolŭ), чехълъ (čexŭlŭ), from Proto-Slavic *čexъlъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čubъ.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian чува́ти (čuváti), from Proto-Slavic *čuvati.

parole.significato: curious, odd, strange (surprisingly out of the ordinary, or unusual)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian чудный (čudnyj), from Proto-Slavic *čudьnъ. By surface analysis, чу́до (čúdo) + -ни́й (-nýj). Compare Russian чудно́й (čudnój).
Inherited from Old East Slavic чудо (čudo), from Proto-Slavic *čudo.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ťuďь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čulъ. Compare Belarusian чу́лы (čúly), Polish czuły.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čuprina, from *čuprъ ~ *čupra + *-ina.
From Old East Slavic чути (čuti), from Proto-Slavic *čuti, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to perceive”), whence English show and caution. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian чути.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čùtъkъ (“attentive, careful”). By surface analysis, чу́ти (čúty) + -ки́й (-kýj).

parole.significato: sense (any of the manners by which living beings perceive the physical world)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čutьje (“perception”). By surface analysis, чу́ти impf (čúty) + -я́ (-já).

parole.significato: to scratch (to rub a surface with a sharp object, especially by a living creature to remove itching with nails, claws,…
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *čexati. Expressive variant of чеса́ти (česáty). Compare Belarusian чу́хаць (čúxacʹ).
From Proto-Slavic *čьxati, from *čixati, of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Russian чиха́ть (čixátʹ), Belarusian чхаць (čxacʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čepъ.

parole.significato: to touch (once, momentarily); to nudge, to poke
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čьpnǫti.
Usually explained as cognate to Russian and Belarusian шаг (šah, “step”), from earlier *сяг (*sjah), from Proto-Slavic *sęgъ.

parole.significato: to roam, to hang about, to hang around
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šastati.

parole.significato: to knock about, to roam, to rove, to wander (to walk around aimlessly)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian шата́тисѧ (šatátisja, “to roam, to wander”), from Old East Slavic шататисѧ (šatatisę, “to roam, to wander”), from Proto-Slavic *šętati sę.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šьvalь (“tailor”). Parsable as Proto-Slavic *šiti (“to sew”) + -аль (-alʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šьvьcь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šelestъ. Compare Russian ше́лест (šélest), Polish szelest, Czech and Slovak šelest.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šьpъtati, of onomatopoeic origin. Cognates include Russian шепта́ть (šeptátʹ), Belarusian шапта́ць (šaptácʹ), Polish szeptać, Bulgarian шептя́ (šeptjá), etc.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šьpъtъ.
Inherited from Old East Slavic сьрсть (sĭrstĭ), шьрсть (šĭrstĭ), from Proto-Slavic *sьrstь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sьrxy.

parole.significato: to hit, to strike, to beat
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian шиба́ти (šibáti), from Old East Slavic шибати (šibati), from Proto-Slavic *šibati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šibenica.
From Proto-Slavic *šestь, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

Inherited from Old East Slavic шило (šilo), from Proto-Slavic *šidlo, composed of *šiti (“to sew”) + *-dlo (“(tool suffix)”). Cognate to Czech šídlo (“awl”) and Latin sūbula (“awl”). By surface analysis, шити (šyty) + -ло (-lo)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šipъ.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian шипшина (šipšina, “dog rose”), from шипокъ (šipok, “dog rose”) + -ина (-ina), from Old East Slavic шипъкъ (šipŭkŭ, “dog rose”), from Proto-Slavic *šipъkъ. Cognate with Belarusian шыпшы́на (šypšýna), Polish szypszyna. Compare also Czech šípek, Russian шипо́вник (šipóvnik)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šȋrь.

parole.significato: width, breadth (the extent or measure of how broad or wide something is)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *širina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *širiti. By surface analysis, шир (šyr, “width, breadth”) + -ити (-yty).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *širokъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šestь na desęte.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šiti, from Proto-Indo-European *syewH-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šišьka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šija.

parole.significato: shell (the hard calcareous covering of an egg)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic скоролупа (skorolupa), скоролупля (skoroluplja), from Proto-Slavic *skorupa and/or *skor(o)lupa.
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *skora (“bast, skin”). Doublet of скора́ (skorá) and шку́ра (škúra).

parole.significato: to whip, to flop, to lash, to scourge
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *smagati, with a common initial с → ш shift, compare шкребти́, штри́кати (škrebtý, štrýkaty). Cognate Polish smagać and probably Lithuanian smõgti (“to strike, to sway”).
Likely from earlier *шморкати (*šmorkaty), from Proto-Slavic *smъrkati. The "а" in the first syllable could've been formed by analogy with Polish smark (“snot”).
From Old East Slavic шеломъ (šelomŭ), from Proto-Slavic *šelmъ. Cognate with Russian шело́м (šelóm) / шлем (šlem), Belarusian шало́м (šalóm).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šestъ.

parole.significato: chink, cleft, crack, crevice, fissure, gap, slit (long narrow opening)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čьpara. Compare Polish szpara.
From Proto-Slavic *čьtyre, reduced form of Proto-Slavic *četyre, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čьtyre na desęte.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čьstiti. Cognate with Russian чти́ть (čtítʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šulьga (“someone with their right hand chopped off; leftie”) from Proto-Indo-European *kseul, *kseoul from Proto-Indo-European *kes-, *kos-, *ks-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šumъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šuma.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šumьnъ. By surface analysis, шум (šum) + -ний (-nyj). Compare Russian шу́мный (šúmnyj), Belarusian шу́мны (šúmny).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šumьnъ. By surface analysis, шумний (šumnyj) + -о (-o). Compare Russian шу́мно (šúmno), Belarusian шу́мны (šúmny).

parole.significato: to make noise, to be noisy
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian шумѣти (šuměti), from Old East Slavic шумѣти (šuměti), from Proto-Slavic *šuměti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *šurь.
From Proto-Slavic *šestь, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.
Melnychuk posits inheritance from Proto-Slavic *ščebьlь. Vasmer associates it with Russian шта́бель (štábelʹ, “stack, pile”) from German Stapel. Compare Polish szczebel, Slovak štebeľ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sьčavь, *sьčavьľь.

parole.significato: to spare, to have mercy on / upon, to mercy, to go easy on (someone)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian щади́ти (ščadíti), from Old East Slavic щадѣти (ščaděti), from Proto-Slavic *ščęditi.

parole.significato: to be lucky, to have luck, to be fortunate, to succeed
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian щасти́ти, счасти́ти (ščastíti, sčastíti), from Proto-Slavic *sъčęstiti. By surface analysis, щастя (ščastja) + -ити (-yty).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian щастьє, щастє (ščastʹje, ščastje), from Old East Slavic съчастиѥ (sŭčastije), from Proto-Slavic *sъčęstьje.
From Proto-Slavic *(j)ešče (“still, yet”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁esk(ʷ)e(h₁). Cognate with Russian ещё (ješčó).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščьbьtъ. From an onomatopoeic root Proto-Slavic *ščьb- + -ет (-et).

parole.significato: to chirrup, to chirp, to tweet, to twitter, to warble
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic щьбьтати (ščĭbĭtati), from Proto-Slavic *ščьbьtati. Compare Russian щебета́ть (ščebetátʹ), Belarusian шчабята́ць (ščabjatácʹ), Polish szczebiotać, Slovene ščebetati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščebьňь, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”).
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ščedrъ.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian щезнути, счезнути (ščeznuti, sčeznuti), from Proto-Slavic *čeznǫti. Cognates include: Russian исче́знуть (isčéznutʹ), Old Polish szczeznać, Bulgarian изчезвам (izčezvam), and Macedonian исчезнува (isčeznuva).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščelpa.

parole.significato: to pinch, to twinge, to ache (to produce sharp pain)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sčemiti.
Inherited from Old East Slavic щенѧ (ščenę), from Proto-Slavic *ščenę.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščьrba.
From щербатий (ščerbatyj) + -ань m (-anʹ). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ščьrba ‹ *sk’r̥b-.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščьrba + -ина (-yna).

parole.significato: bristles (of animal hair or a brush)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *(š)četina.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščigъlъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščikokoltъka.

parole.significato: to pinch (to squeeze a small amount of a person's skin and flesh, making it hurt)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščipati. Cognate with Serbo-Croatian штипати, Czech štípat, Russian щипать (ščipatʹ)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščirъ.
From щир (ščyr) + -и́ця (-ýcja), from Proto-Slavic *ščirъ.

From Old East Slavic щитъ (ščitŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ščitъ (“shield”), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *skeita, from Proto-Indo-European *skey-to-m, from *skey- (“to cut, separate”). Cognate with Serbo-Croatian štit, Old Irish scíath, Latin scūtum.
From Proto-Slavic *čьto, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, *kʷís.
From Proto-Slavic *ščeka. Cognate with Belarusian шчака́ (ščaká) and Russian щека́ (ščeká).

parole.significato: weak and skinny, scrawny and frail
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian щуплый (ščuplyj), from Old East Slavic щуплъ (ščuplŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ščuplъ.

parole.significato: chink, cleft, crack, crevice, fissure, gap, slit (long narrow opening)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščelina. By surface analysis, щіль (ščilʹ) + -ина (-yna).
From Proto-Slavic *(š)četъka, *sъčetь.

parole.significato: to tempt, to entice, to instigate
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *juditi.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *junakъ. From Proto-Slavic *junъ (“young”) + *-akъ (masculine nominalizing suffix). Cognate with Bulgarian юна́к (junák), Czech jonák (Moravian junák), Polish junak.

parole.significato: youth, adolescence (young age; period of life before maturity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *junostь. By surface analysis, ю́ний (júnyj) + -ість (-istʹ). Compare Russian ю́ность (júnostʹ), Belarusian ю́насць (júnascʹ).
From Proto-Slavic *juxa (“soup”), distantly related to English juice.
From older form яз (jaz), язъ (jaz), from Old East Slavic ꙗзъ (jazŭ), from Proto-Slavic *(j)azъ. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *éǵh₂.
From Old Ruthenian ꙗ́блоко (jábloko), ꙗ́блуко (jábluko), from Old East Slavic ꙗблъко (jablŭko), from Proto-Slavic *àblъko.

parole.significato: apple tree (any cultivar of the Malus domestica tree)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *abloňa. By surface analysis, я́блунь (jáblunʹ) + -а (-a).

parole.significato: to show, to reveal, to present
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ꙗви́ти (javíti), from Old East Slavic ꙗвити (javiti), from Proto-Slavic *aviti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *avьnъ. By surface analysis, я́ва (jáva) + -ний (-nyj).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ꙗ́воръ (jávor), from Proto-Slavic *avorъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *agniti sę.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *agnica. By surface analysis, ягня́ (jahnjá) + -и́ця (-ýcja). Compare тели́ця (telýcja).
Inherited from Old East Slavic агнѧ (agnę), ꙗгнѧ (jagnę), from Proto-Slavic *agnę, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷnós.

parole.significato: lamb (flesh of a lamb used as food)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *agnętina. By surface analysis, ягня́та (jahnjáta, “lambs”) + -ина (-yna, suffix denoting a type of meat).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ꙗ҆́года (ja҆́hoda), from Old East Slavic ꙗгода (jagoda), from Proto-Slavic *agoda, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ṓˀgāˀ.

parole.significato: berry (attributive) (of, relating to or made of berries)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *agodьnъ. By surface analysis, я́года (jáhoda) + -ний (-nyj). Compare Russian я́годный (jágodnyj), Belarusian я́гадны (jáhadny).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ꙗдъ, ѣдъ (jad, jěd), from Old East Slavic ꙗдъ, ѣдъ (jadŭ, jědŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ědъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ędro.
From Proto-Slavic *aduxa. Cognate with Polish jaducha.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *adušьlivъ. By surface analysis, яду́ха (jadúxa) + -ливий (-lyvyj).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ѧзы́къ (jazýk), from Old East Slavic ѧзꙑкъ (językŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ęzykъ, from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s.
From Old East Slavic ꙗице (jaice), from Proto-Slavic *ājьcè, diminutive of *ȃje (“egg”), ultimately from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ṓjan (“egg”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm (“egg”).
From Old East Slavic ꙗко (jako), from Proto-Slavic *jako.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jakъ.

parole.significato: spruce (any of various large coniferous evergreen trees of the genus Picea)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ȅdlь. By surface analysis, яль (jalʹ) (obsolete) + -ина (-yna).
From Proto-Slavic *jalovъ (“infertile”), from Proto-Indo-European *jal- (“bad”).

parole.significato: juniper (any shrub or tree of the genus Juniperus of the cypress family)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jalovьcь. Compare Russian я́ловец (jálovec), Polish jałowiec, Czech jalovec.
From Old East Slavic ꙗма (jama), from Proto-Slavic *jama.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jarъ (“furious”)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jarъ (“spring”)
From Old East Slavic ꙗрьмъ (jarĭmŭ), from Proto-Slavic *arьmo.

parole.significato: spring, springtime (of agricultural labour, crops, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jarovъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jarostь (“fury”).

parole.significato: ash, ash tree (tree of the genus Fraxinus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *àsenь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *asenь.
From dialectal Proto-Slavic *ěskyni. Cognate with Polish jaskinia.
From Proto-Slavic *ěskravъ (“sparky”). Related to Proto-Slavic *jьskra (“a spark”), *ěsknъ (“clear”). Cognate with Belarusian яскравы (jaskravy), Polish jaskrawy, Upper Sorbian jaskrawy.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ꙗсли (jasli), from Proto-Slavic *jasli. Cognate with Russian я́сли (jásli).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *dęsna.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ěsnъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ěsniti. By surface analysis, ясни́й (jasnýj) + -ити (-yty).
From Proto-Slavic *ěsnostь, from *ěsnъ. By surface analysis, я́сний (jásnyj) + -ість (-istʹ). Compare Russian я́сность (jásnostʹ), Belarusian я́снасць (jásnascʹ), Polish jasność.
From Proto-Slavic *ętry, with -івка (-ivka). Compare Belarusian ятро́ўка (jatrówka).

parole.significato: barley (annual temperate grasses of the species Hordeum vulgare)
parole.testo: From Old East Slavic ѩчьнѣнъ (jęčĭněnŭ), Old East Slavic ѩчьмꙑ (jęčĭmy), from Proto-Slavic *ęčьmy. Cognate with Russian ячме́нь (jačménʹ).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *aščerъka.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ȃjьčьnikъ. By surface analysis, яйце́ (jajcé) + -ник (-nyk).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian єти (jeti), from Old East Slavic ети (jeti), from Proto-Slavic *jetì (“to copulate”). Cognate with Russian е́ть (jétʹ), ети́ (jetí), Old Novgorodian ѥти (jeti), Ancient Greek οἴφω (oíphō), Sanskrit यभति (yábhati).

From Middle Ukrainian и (y), from Proto-Slavic *i, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey, an early locative singular determiner, formed from the root *h₁e-, *h₁o-. Compare Ancient Greek εἰ (ei, “if”), Gothic 𐌴𐌹 (ei, “and, so that, be it”).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьvьlga.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьgo.

parole.significato: izgoi (in Kievan Rus, an individual excluded from a particular social status)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old East Slavic изгои (izgoi) or изгой (izgoj). By surface analysis, із- (iz-) + го́їти (hójity), from Proto-Slavic *gojiti (“to heal, feed”), the latter derived from a causative form of Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”) (whence жи́ти (žýty)).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьkati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъlъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьkra.
From Old East Slavic имѧ (imę), from Proto-Slavic *jьmę.

parole.significato: to name, to denominate, to call
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian именовати (imenovati), from Old East Slavic именовати (imenovati), from Proto-Slavic *jьmenovati.
From Proto-Slavic *mьgla, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃migʰleh₂ (“mist, cloud”). Cognate with Russian мгла (mgla).

parole.significato: differently, in a different way, otherwise
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *jьnako, інакший (inakšyj) + -е (-e)
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьnъde.
From the comparative of Proto-Slavic *(j)inъ. Cognate with Russian ино́й (inój), Belarusian іншы (inšy).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьnьjь.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *rъďa.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ржа́ти (ržáti), from Old East Slavic ръзати (rŭzati), from Proto-Slavic *rъzati.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьskra.

parole.significato: capital, principal (initial amount of money or property, excluding profit or interest)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *jьstъ (“true, real, actual”). Cognate with і́стина (ístyna) and істо́та (istóta). The semantic shift is from "actual property/money" to "principal sum" or "capital".
From Old East Slavic ити (iti), from Proto-Slavic *jьti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éyti.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian єбати (jebati), from Old East Slavic ѥбати (jebati), from Proto-Slavic *jebati.
Inherited from Old East Slavic ѣдъ (jědŭ), from Proto-Slavic *ědъ.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ěda.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian ѣдло (jědlo) or идло (idlo), from Proto-Slavic *ědlo.
Likely a later innovation, from їд (jid) + -ь (-ʹ), from Proto-Slavic *ědъ.
From Proto-Slavic *ěďa, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ḗˀdjāˀ.
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ežь. Cognate with Belarusian во́жык (vóžyk), Russian ёжик (jóžik).
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ězda.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ězditi.
From Proto-Slavic *ěsti, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *ēˀstei, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jixъ.

parole.significato: to go (by vehicle), to drive, to ride
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ěxati.
Inherited from Old Ruthenian єѣ (jejě), from Old East Slavic ѥѣ (jejě), from Proto-Slavic *jeję̇, North Slavic genitive feminine of Proto-Slavic *jь.

Voiced from earlier ки́кнути (kýknuty), from кик (kyk, “death (vulgar)”) + -нути (-nuty), from Proto-Slavic *kykъ (“crook, a certain crooked thing; death (figuratively, taboo)”), from Proto-Indo-European *kew- (“to bend, to crook”), extended to *kew-k. For the semantic development of "crook → death"

parole.significato: goo, gum (sticky substance exuded by certain plants)
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *glьjь.

parole.significato: lump (a nodule of tissue under the skin as a result of injury)
parole.testo: From Proto-Slavic *gulja from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“"to bend, to curve"”). Related to Polish kula (“ball”) and Ukrainian ку́ля (kúlja, “ball, sphere”).
From Bukovinian regional pronunciation of дідо, the Western Ukrainian variant of the Standard Ukrainian дід (grandfather), from Proto-Slavic *dědъ.

parole.significato: appended to nouns, adjectives and verbs to form masculine nouns of various meanings;
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-akъ, or from Old East Slavic -акъ (-akŭ).

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from nouns; -ish, -y.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьnъ or *-jь.

parole.significato: a being/thing with a given characteristic; often of a colloquial nature: -er
parole.testo: Probably from soft stem + -а́к (-ák).

parole.significato: to roam, to rove, to wander
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *blǫkati, from *blǫditi (“to err”) + *-kati. Erich Berneker suggested a possible influence from *lǫkъ (“bow”) / *oblǫkъ (“arch”). Grigory Ilyinsky alternatively hypothesized a metanalysis of Proto-Slavic *ob- + *lǫkati (“to bow, to bend”), meaning "to deviate from the pat
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brudьnъ or possibly borrowed from Polish brudny.

parole.significato: to own, to possess, to have, to be in possession of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian владати (vladati), which simultaneously derives from both Old Church Slavonic владати (vladati) and Old Polish władać. Alternatively, a later borrowing from Church Slavonic directly into Ukrainian. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *voldati. Doublet of воло́дати (volódaty).

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian вовъторъкъ (vovtork), овъторъкъ (ovtork), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *vъtorъkъ. Compare Belarusian аўто́рак (awtórak). The word likely received prothetic "о" at some point, though the source of this vowel is unknown. Sometimes alternatively explained as being equiva

parole.significato: to greet, to hail, to salute
parole.testo: Either borrowed from Polish witać, from Proto-Slavic *vitati or arose as a reanalyzation of приві́т (pryvít) "hello, hi" → приві́тати (pryvítaty) → віта́ти (vitáty), in which case came from Proto-Slavic *větъ "agreement". Doublet of вита́ти (vytáty, “soar, dwell”).

From Proto-Slavic *duma (“thought, care, council”), Origin disputed. Either from Germanic, possibly Proto-Germanic *dōmaz (“judicial decision, act, thought”), Gothic 𐌳𐍉𐌼𐍃 (dōms, “judgment, act, thought”), 𐌳𐍉𐌼𐌾𐌰𐌽 (dōmjan, “to judge”), 𐌳𐍉𐌼 (dōm, “council, thought”). Also compare modern German -tum, En

parole.significato: poker (metal rod for adjusting burning logs or coals in a fire)
parole.testo: According to Vasmer, inherited from a Proto-Slavic form, probably with the original sense of “stump, stalk”; compare Russian кочерга́ (kočergá), кучу́рга (kučúrga), Polish koczarga, Belarusian качарга́ (kačarhá), Russian коко́ра (kokóra), коча́н (kočán). Alternatively (but less likely), perhaps a Tu

Inherited from Old East Slavic мьстьникъ (mĭstĭnikŭ, “avenger”), from Proto-Slavic *mьstьnikъ (“avenger”). By surface analysis, (obsolete) месть (mestʹ, “vengeance”) + -ник (-nyk) or from (rare) ме́сний (mésnyj, “vengeful”) + -ик (-yk). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic мьстьникъ (mĭstĭnikŭ).

Per ESSJa, inherited from Proto-Slavic *mitь, related to Proto-Slavic *mitě, *mitъ, *mimo, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“change”). Alternatively, from earlier меть (metʹ, “throw, sweep, motion”), from мета́ти (metáty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian нижъ, нѣжъ, нежъ (niž, něž, než), all of which derive from either Proto-Slavic *ni že or *ne že, or both at the same time. Compare Czech než, Polish niż, Belarusian ніж (niž), (archaic) Russian не́же (néže), (archaic) Bulgarian не́же (néže), Old Church Slavonic неже (než
Either borrowed from Polish pierwszy or formed in an analogous manner; in either case, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *pьrvъ. Cognates include Belarusian пе́ршы (pjéršy) and Polish pierwszy.

parole.significato: to see off, to see to (accompany someone to a point of departure)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian провадити (provaditi), from Old East Slavic провадити (provaditi), probably from проводити (provoditi) with о → а under the influence of проважати (provažati), or possibly related to Proto-Slavic *vaditi.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian розумѣ́ти (rozumě́ti), from Old East Slavic розумѣти (rozuměti), from Proto-Slavic *orzuměti. By surface analysis, розум (rozum) + -і́ти (-íty) or alternatively роз- (roz-) + умі́ти (umíty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian росомаха (rosomaxa), with further etymology unclear. Possibly arising from a taboo metathesis from Proto-Slavic *sormaxa. Alternatively, Kiparsky and Räsänen posited connections with Uralic languages.
From Old East Slavic стѧгъ (stęgŭ), which was formed either from Old Norse stǫng, or from Proto-Slavic *stěgъ.

parole.significato: to come to one's senses, to recover one's senses, to regain one's senses (to become reasonable, comprehending, or respo…
parole.testo: Melnychuk posits a borrowing from Middle High German schamen (“to feel ashamed”). Alternatively derived from Proto-Slavic *sъ‑xa‑menǫti sę, which Melnychuk finds less convincing. Compare Belarusian схамяну́цца (sxamjanúcca).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; Probably; alternatively
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian триво́га, трыво́га (trivóha, tryvóha) (att. in 1574), initially attested as трво́га (trvóha) in 1538, most likely from Old Polish trwoga, of uncertain origin, possibly from *trъvati. Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оупъвати (upŭvati), either via Old Ruthenian упова́ти, вповати (upováti, vpovati) and Old East Slavic оупъвати (upŭvati) or borrowed later from Church Slavonic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *upъvati.

From Proto-Slavic *xolča, *xolša, *kolša, thought to be borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin calcea. Compare Belarusian кало́ша (kalóša, “trouser/pant leg”), Serbo-Croatian hlȁče pl (“trousers, pants”). Alternatively related to Proto-Slavic *xoliti.
